Helena's accusation turns her into a fugitive from the agency she intends to reclaim. Heir-director Strategist Magi IND · 002 Chibi preview Hidden contingency Kyrien Independent Opening MSF Later director A failed assassin forced into secret service by Lynleit, he masters intelligence tradecraft until a coerced MSF association becomes his answer to magic. Tradecraft Survival Intelligence MSF · 003 Chibi preview Accusation architect Helena MSF Fionn's wife and Lynleit's stepmother, she frames his biological daughter for his assassination and seizes control of MSF. IND · 004 Chibi preview Secret bodyguard Tien Independent Helena's concealed mercenary and assassin, tasked with protecting her and removing enemies quietly and cleanly. Kyrien becomes Tien's direct operational rival. ARC · 005 Chibi preview Pivotal figure Fionn MSF Magiarchy Lynleit's biological father and Helena's husband. His elimination becomes the fulcrum for the accusation against his daughter and the hunt for her arrest. FLD · 006 Chibi preview Ducal Guard field agent Heyk Government The sole survivor of a paramilitary unit massacred inside Vilen's park, he enters Drake and Sherie's service carrying grief for his squad. FLD · 007 Chibi preview Diplomat in training Sherie Government Her first independent strategy secures the secret MSF negotiations, after which she expects praise and pampering from her reluctant mentor. FLD · 008 Chibi preview Official for Special Assignments Drake Government A State Councillor by rank and elite troubleshooter by office, he carries delegated authority into sensitive investigations and diplomatic errands. ARC · 009 Chibi preview Communications specialist Felix MSF A playful hacker and communications specialist who bypasses obvious barriers, disrupts hostile systems, and opens routes for the field team. ARC · 010 Chibi preview Protection specialist Reiner MSF A stern, powerfully built protection specialist who anchors the field team, holds exposed positions, and applies force directly. ARC · 011 Chibi preview Procedural investigator Yulia Independent A top criminology student whose meticulous method checks Hiyu's wild theories, even when reluctant loyalty follows him into the quarantined park. ARC · 012 Chibi preview Intuitive investigator Hiyu Independent A criminology student whose appetite for impossible explanations sends him into the quarantined park with a reluctant Yulia beside him. ARC · 013 Chibi preview Independent magical examiner Natalia Private Eye Magiarchy Former Academy A former professor whose paid investigations finance independent research into magical deviations, personal afflictions, and edge cases. ARC · 014 L Chibi unavailable Demiholumn ally Lester Independent Half human and half Holumn, Lester assists Natalia independently and sometimes accomplishes the impossible for her cases. ARC · 015 Chibi preview Academy student Myka Magi Academy Magiarchy Natalia's niece and frequent confidante, learning formal magecraft while relying on her aunt for advice that reaches beyond Academy doctrine. PLC · 016 IL Chibi unavailable Police inspector Inspector Leo Police A police inspector newly registered in the roster. Detailed role, history, and visual profile remain to be defined. entries.title: After the Failed Attempt
entries.subtitle: Chapter 03 · The Hidden Wager
entries.text: After the Failed Attempt Chapter 03 · The Hidden Wager After Kyrien's failed attack on an MSF-protected politician nearly harms Lynleit, she questions him without revealing that she was present and converts his prison risk into a secret alliance. Kyrien's attempt on an MSF-protected politician fails because the target secretly belongs to the Magi world. Lynleit is present and almost harmed during the attempt, but Kyrien does not know she was there and she never tells him. Lynleit takes control of his interrogation and offers conditional freedom in exchange for becoming her secret helper. She recruits him because her intuition warns her that a danger she cannot yet identify is approaching. Lynleit later tells only Felix and Reiner, while even Fionn remains outside the compartment. Reiner trusts Lynleit's judgment, while Felix accepts the decision without trusting Kyrien. Chapter 03: After the Failed Attempt Placeholder draft built only from confirmed scene facts. The dialogue, location details, and connective action will be replaced or revised when final chapter material is available. The Protection Failure The politician is under MSF protection when Kyrien makes the attempt. It fails for a reason he could not have anticipated: the target belongs to the hidden world of Magi. Lynleit is present during the attempt and is almost harmed by it. Kyrien does not know she was there. Lynleit never tells him. The Interview Room Kyrien now faces prison, and the police office gives him no reason to expect another outcome. Lynleit enters the interrogation knowing that the man opposite her nearly injured or killed her without intending to. To Kyrien, the personal edge in her questions has no visible source. Lynleit enters the interrogation with authority that has not yet been explained. She does not offer forgiveness. She offers conditional freedom. Kyrien may avoid prison if he becomes her secret helper. The arrangement leaves him confined to her demands, useful precisely because Helena does not know he belongs to Lynleit's circle. The Warning Lynleit cannot prove that a crisis is coming. Her suspicion of Helena is built from a tense family history, things she has noticed but not yet explained, and an intuition that tells her the present balance will not hold. Recruiting Kyrien is a high-risk answer to a danger she cannot name. Fionn's assassination is still far away. Lynleit does not foresee the event itself, but she acts with the conviction that she will soon need an ally her enemies cannot anticipate. The Compartment Lynleit later tells only Felix and Reiner. Even Fionn remains uninformed. Both friends see Kyrien as a possible danger to her. Reiner accepts the arrangement because he trusts Lynleit's judgment. Felix yields because Reiner's decision leaves him in the minority, but his distrust of Kyrien remains. The wager stays hidden. Much later, when Fionn is assassinated and Helena moves against Lynleit, the danger she sensed finally takes visible form. Lynleit,Kyrien,Felix,Reiner

entries.title: Before the First Bell
entries.subtitle: Chapter 01 · Vanishing Point
entries.text: Before the First Bell Chapter 01 · Vanishing Point Lynleit and Fionn attend private negotiations at a church before dawn while their MSF escort waits outside and wonders why. Lynleit and Fionn arrive at a church before dawn for private negotiations. Felix and Reiner wait outside as the family's security detail. Lynleit leaves the meeting early and visibly irritated. Felix and Reiner seek gossip, but Lynleit redirects them with a playful tease. A report of another disappearance appears while the meeting is in progress. Chapter 01: Before the First Bell Working draft based on the confirmed opening scene. Dialogue and exact staging remain provisional. 05:17 The first week of September had arrived without deciding whether it belonged to summer or autumn. The city was dark when the MSF car turned onto Saint Orison Street. Rain from the previous night still rested in the joins between the stones, and the church at the end of the road seemed to have collected more darkness than the buildings around it. Its windows were unlit. Its bell had not yet marked the hour. Felix slowed at the iron gate. "This is the address?" Reiner checked the card in his hand for the third time. "Saint Orison Cathedral. East entrance." "A cathedral. At this hour." From the rear seat, Lynleit looked past them toward the steps. She had said little since they left MSF headquarters. Her coat was buttoned neatly, her expression composed, and the file resting across her knees had not been opened once. Fionn sat beside her with his eyes closed. "The east entrance," he said. Felix glanced at the empty street. "Of course. Much less suspicious than the front." Lynleit looked at him through the mirror. "Your gift for discretion remains one of the agency's better-kept secrets." "Thank you." "That was not praise." "I accepted it before the correction." Reiner hid a smile behind the route card. They drove around the cathedral and stopped beside a narrow door set into the oldest part of the stonework. A priest was already waiting beneath the arch. He wore no coat despite the cold. Fionn stepped out first. Lynleit followed, taking the file with her. Felix reached for his door. The priest raised one hand. "The officers will remain outside." Felix paused with the door half open. "We are their security detail." "You are expected to wait." Reiner looked to Fionn. "Director?" Fionn did not appear surprised. "Stay with the car." "Sir, if this is a negotiation, we should at least clear the room." "The room has already been cleared." The priest opened the door. Warm amber light touched the wet stones, then narrowed as Fionn entered. Lynleit stopped before following him. "Try not to investigate the clergy while we are inside," she said. Felix leaned against the open car door. "How long will you be?" "I don't know. Stay warm." Then she disappeared into the church, and the door closed behind her. Outside At 05:31, Felix decided the meeting concerned money. At 05:38, he revised this to blackmail. At 05:46, after a delivery van passed without stopping and a light appeared in one high window, he proposed that Fionn had joined a secret monastic order and intended to leave MSF to Lynleit before breakfast. Reiner remained beside the car, arms folded. "You could ask him when he comes out." "And spoil it?" Across the street, a newspaper bundle landed outside a closed kiosk. The top page loosened in the wind. For a moment, Felix could read part of the headline. SECOND VOLUNTEER MISSING NEAR VILEN PARKLAND The page folded over itself before he could see the rest. "They closed another path through the park," he said. Reiner followed his glance. "Drainage works." "In September?" "Rain happens in September." "People also happen in September. They usually do not vanish into landscaping projects." Reiner looked back toward the church door. "You are supposed to be watching the entrance." Felix sighed and obeyed. The bell still had not rung. An Early Exit At 05:53, the side door opened. Lynleit came out alone. She descended the steps with the same measured pace she used when crossing the operations floor, but the file was now held too tightly beneath one arm. Her mouth was set. Felix straightened. Reiner opened the rear door for her. "Is the Director following?" "Eventually." She did not get into the car. Felix and Reiner exchanged a look. Lynleit noticed it immediately. "No," she said. Felix placed a hand against his chest. "I have not asked anything." "You have asked several things. You simply used your face." "Then my face would appreciate clarification. Why is the director of an intelligence foundation negotiating with a church before sunrise?" "Perhaps he is confessing the budget." "Reiner said money too." "I said no such thing," Reiner replied. Felix continued. "We were refused entry. The priest knew we were coming. You left early, and you look as though somebody inside suggested something very stupid with complete confidence." Lynleit looked back at the closed door. She turned back to them. "You are both remarkably interested in private church business." "Occupational concern," Felix said. "Of course. Should I ask whether the priest has time to arrange a ceremony for you? You are already dressed, and Reiner has spent the entire morning pretending not to enjoy your company." Reiner went still. Felix smiled. "Would MSF cover the reception?" "Only if you classify it as a training exercise." "I object to this entire conversation," Reiner said. "Noted," Lynleit replied. "Felix, put his objection in the wedding file." "We have a wedding file?" "We do now." The cathedral bell struck once. The side door opened again, and Fionn stepped into the morning with the priest behind him. Whatever expression he had worn inside was gone before he reached the first step. He looked from Lynleit to Felix, then to Reiner. "Did I miss something?" "Felix and Reiner are considering a church wedding," Lynleit said. "We are not," Reiner replied. Fionn considered this with the gravity of an official report. "Then I appear to have missed very little." He entered the car. Lynleit followed without looking back at the church. As Felix pulled away from the curb, the morning traffic reports announced a new diversion around the park. The explanation was maintenance. The estimated reopening date was left unspecified. Nobody in the car commented on it. Lynleit,Fionn,Felix,Reiner

entries.title: Doom Has an Address · Version 1 · Alternate
entries.subtitle: Chapter 07 · Lynleit Disappears
entries.text: Doom Has an Address · Version 1 · Alternate Chapter 07 · Lynleit Disappears After jointly destroying a Holumn, Lynleit and Kyrien inherit one fatal curse written across both identities and search for a way to survive without sacrificing either life. Lynleit and Kyrien destroy a Holumn together and complete the final condition of its mechanism. The Holumn transfers one terminal curse across both of their identities, causing progressive physical decline and a prognosis measured first in weeks and then in days. Suppressing the curse in either person fails because the remaining half reconstructs the other. The traditional solution requires one of them to die first so the surviving identity is released. Lynleit rejects that answer and searches Magiarchal, medical, theurgical, academic, and Church records for another form of identity discontinuity. Natalia identifies the attachment as sympathetic recognition of the ego and proposes profound reciprocal transformation as a possible alternative to death. Father Mikhail reaches the same conclusion through Church records and tells Lynleit that physical intimacy could work only if an existing attachment changes both identities. Lynleit withholds Natalia and Mikhail's proposed treatment from Kyrien. Lynleit initiates an awkward sexual encounter and Kyrien responds. Their reciprocal change makes the curse unable to recognize the exact pair of identities that destroyed the Holumn, causing the entanglement to fracture. Lynleit hiding the notebook page suggests that she still cannot discuss the attempt openly with Kyrien. inferred Doom Has an Address After the killing For several nights after they destroyed the Holumn, Lynleit blamed her exhaustion on the fight. Then small cuts stopped closing. Sleep left her as tired as she had been before it. Kyrien began pausing on stairs. He waited for her at the landings, which might have been considerate if she had not seen him trying to recover his breath. The examinations gave them weeks. Suppressing the curse in Lynleit brought brief relief. It returned through Kyrien. Treating him produced the same result in reverse. Whatever had followed them out of the fight was attached to both of them. One could survive if the other died first. "No," Lynleit said. She took the reports away and began calling people who had not yet given her that answer. The Magiarchal records led her to physicians, prohibited theurgical procedures, and arguments about what counted as a person. Memory erasure would not work. Neither would a coma. Destroying magical capacity offered no reliable prospect, and having someone declared dead would change nothing. Eventually she called Natalia. The former professor Natalia was silent long enough that Lynleit checked the connection. "I'm reading," she said. "You sent six reports." "The last two are the same treatment. On different patients." "I noticed." Lynleit leaned against the desk. Her hand had begun trembling again. She put the telephone in the other one. "The Holumn transferred its death to whoever killed it," Natalia said. "You killed it together. That's why treating either of you separately fails." "They've established that." "They've established what happens. I'm asking what it recognizes." Lynleit looked at the reports. "Us." "Your bodies? Your names? The people you understand yourselves to be?" She had used that tone in lectures. Lynleit had once liked being the student who could answer her. "The ego," she said. "Good. Now tell me why it has to be destroyed." "Because it keeps reconstructing the curse." "And death is the only thing that can change a person?" Lynleit stopped looking at the reports. Natalia spoke about substitute kings, human-shaped vessels used in purification rites, and stories in which a life was hidden outside its body. Lynleit let her finish the first example, interrupted the second, and had to ask her to repeat the third. "These aren't your curse," Natalia said. "But the point of attachment isn't always where you'd expect. Something can recognize a role or a relationship. In this case it recognizes the two people responsible for one act." "Could we make it recognize someone else?" "You need to stop being the people it recognizes." "Memory erasure doesn't work." "Because your memories aren't all of you. Nor is your title, or your name, or the description you'd give a stranger. Jung's ego isn't the whole psyche either, but it is a useful place to begin: the conscious sense of who you are. That can change without killing you." "How much would we have to change?" "That I don't know." Lynleit rubbed her forehead. "Conversion," Natalia continued. "Grief. Parenthood, sometimes. An experience that makes your old assumptions impossible to live by. The trouble is getting there deliberately, and getting both of you there before the curse restores what you've changed." "We're already confronting death." "I was hoping for something you could survive." "Then suggest it." Natalia went quiet. "No," Lynleit said. "I haven't said anything." "You were about to." "I was." "Natalia." "Fall in love." Lynleit took the telephone away from her ear and looked at it. "You cannot possibly be serious." "I am." "You've taken me through death rituals and Carl Jung to tell me to fall in love?" "You asked for an alternative." "I asked for something we can do." "And I can't prescribe it. You can't pretend your way out of this. But if you already matter enough to each other, there may be something to work with." Lynleit looked toward the door. "How would we know?" "You'd have to risk finding out." There were faster possibilities, Natalia admitted. She declined to describe them. "Go speak to a priest." A second opinion Father Mikhail had records Natalia could not consult. He laid them out while Lynleit took notes. Conversion had broken one attachment. Marriage had broken another. Other accounts concerned war, parenthood, and a confession followed by absolution that had only partly succeeded. Lynleit put a mark beside the partial result. "So confession isn't enough." "In that case, no." "And marriage?" "Neither is a certificate." She looked up. "These people changed," he said. "The records tell us when. They don't give us a rite that will make it happen to you." The list occupied most of a page. She had already crossed out more than half of it. "What would you recommend for Kyrien and me?" Mikhail looked at her notebook, then at her. "Just have sex, loser." Lynleit became red from her throat to her ears. "What?" "You heard me." "You are a priest." "An observant one." She stood and took her coat. "Lynleit. There are theological reasons." She reached the door. "Sex is not the important part." Her hand remained on the handle. "If the attachment is already there, acting on it may change what you are to each other. Enough to break the recognition. I cannot promise you that it will." "And if it doesn't?" "Then you will merely have had sex." She left before he could add anything. In the corridor she discovered that she had written SEX? across the middle of her notebook. She nearly tore the page out. Days Kyrien knew the prognosis and the failed treatments. When he asked about her research, she told him she was still checking something. She checked it against a Magiarchal text, then a thaumaturgical paper. Neither gave her a dependable way to measure the change. Both gave her reasons to keep thinking about it. She tried to imagine explaining the proposed treatment to Kyrien. She got as far as his expression and shut the notebook. By then he tired after ordinary errands. She had to steady her wrist to write. Their remaining time was measured in days. The evening Kyrien noticed the second change of clothes. "Are we going somewhere?" "No." "Then why..." "Is there something wrong with this?" He stopped asking. Later she corrected him over something that needed no correction and spent several minutes avoiding his eyes. "Is this about the curse?" A cushion hit him in the face. He lowered it. "Lynleit." "Don't." "I asked a question." "Ask another one." She had expected to recognize the right moment. Instead they sat beside each other on the sofa, tired and frightened, discussing something she could not keep her mind on. Kyrien said her name. She looked at him. Then she moved closer before she could find another reason to wait. He was surprised. She gave him time to understand, and he answered her. The encounter that followed was sudden and awkward, with little of the composure she had imagined bringing to it. The curse became unstable while they were together. For several seconds they felt it searching for something in them, returning to the same place and failing to settle. Its hold fractured. Neither had cast a spell. Their attachment had changed both identities enough to disrupt the curse's recognition. The encounter had brought that change about; it had no curative power of its own. They survived. Lynleit still had the page in her notebook. She folded it under the next one before Kyrien could see. Lynleit,Kyrien,Natalia,Father Mikhail

"You killed it together. That's why treating either of you separately fails." "They've established that." "They've established what happens. I'm asking what it recognizes." Lynleit looked at the reports. "Us." "Your bodies? Your names? The people you understand yourselves to be?" She had used that tone in lectures. Lynleit had once liked being the student who could answer her. "The ego," she said. "Good. Now tell me why it has to be destroyed." "Because it keeps reconstructing the curse." "And death is the only thing that can change a person?" Lynleit stopped looking at the reports. Natalia spoke about substitute kings, human-shaped vessels used in purification rites, and stories in which a life was hidden outside its body. Lynleit let her finish the first example, interrupted the second, and had to ask her to repeat the third. "These aren't your curse," Natalia said. "But the point of attachment isn't always where you'd expect. Something can recognize a role or a relationship. In this case it recognizes the two people responsible for one act." "Could we make it recognize someone else?" "You need to stop being the people it recognizes." "Memory erasure doesn't work." "Because your memories aren't all of you. Nor is your title, or your name, or the description you'd give a stranger. Jung's ego isn't the whole psyche either, but it is a useful place to begin: the conscious sense of who you are. That can change without killing you." "How much would we have to change?" "That I don't know." Lynleit rubbed her forehead. "Conversion," Natalia continued. "Grief. Parenthood, sometimes. An experience that makes your old assumptions impossible to live by. The trouble is getting there deliberately, and getting both of you there before the curse restores what you've changed." "We're already confronting death." "I was hoping for something you could survive." "Then suggest it." Natalia went quiet. "No," Lynleit said. "I haven't said anything." "You were about to." "I was." "Natalia." "Fall in love." Lynleit took the telephone away from her ear and looked at it. "You cannot possibly be serious." "I am." "You've taken me through death rituals and Carl Jung to tell me to fall in love?" "You asked for an alternative." "I asked for something we can do." "And I can't prescribe it. You can't pretend your way out of this. But if you already matter enough to each other, there may be something to work with." Lynleit looked toward the door. "How would we know?" "You'd have to risk finding out." There were faster possibilities, Natalia admitted. She declined to describe them. "Go speak to a priest." A second opinion Father Mikhail had records Natalia could not consult. He laid them out while Lynleit took notes. Conversion had broken one attachment. Marriage had broken another. Other accounts concerned war, parenthood, and a confession followed by absolution that had only partly succeeded. Lynleit put a mark beside the partial result. "So confession isn't enough." "In that case, no." "And marriage?" "Neither is a certificate." She looked up. "These people changed," he said. "The records tell us when. They don't give us a rite that will make it happen to you." The list occupied most of a page. She had already crossed out more than half of it. "What would you recommend for Kyrien and me?" Mikhail looked at her notebook, then at her. "Just have sex, loser." Lynleit became red from her throat to her ears. "What?" "You heard me." "You are a priest." "An observant one." She stood and took her coat. "Lynleit. There are theological reasons." She reached the door. "Sex is not the important part." Her hand remained on the handle. "If the attachment is already there, acting on it may change what you are to each other. Enough to break the recognition. I cannot promise you that it will." "And if it doesn't?" "Then you will merely have had sex." She left before he could add anything. In the corridor she discovered that she had written SEX? across the middle of her notebook. She nearly tore the page out. Days Kyrien knew the prognosis and the failed treatments. When he asked about her research, she told him she was still checking something. She checked it against a Magiarchal text, then a thaumaturgical paper. Neither gave her a dependable way to measure the change. Both gave her reasons to keep thinking about it. She tried to imagine explaining the proposed treatment to Kyrien. She got as far as his expression and shut the notebook. By then he tired after ordinary errands. She had to steady her wrist to write. Their remaining time was measured in days. Two days later Natalia called while Lynleit was reading. "So." "No." "I haven't asked anything." "You were about to." "I was." Lynleit kept her eyes on the page. "How do you feel about Kyrien now?" "The same." "Nothing changed?" "Nothing relevant." "Interesting distinction." "There is no distinction." Lynleit turned a page she had not read. "The curse is gone," she said. "Yes." "We're alive. The intervention accomplished its purpose." "I thought you said the attempt failed." "It did." "Then it wasn't necessary to finish." Lynleit closed the book. "There will not be another attempt." "I didn't suggest one." "There is no reason for one." "Correct." "The matter is resolved." Natalia let her wait. "There is absolutely no reason for Kyrien and me to repeat anything that happened that evening." "I agree." "Good." Another silence. Then Natalia asked, "Are you disappointed?" Lynleit hung up. The book was open again before she remembered that she had lost her place. She went back a page. That one was unfamiliar too. The missing explanation Kyrien knew she had tried to sleep with him. He had not known she could approach it with quite so much anger. The curse had begun weakening the following morning. Now it was gone. When he asked her about that evening, she refused to explain. When he mentioned the improvement, she said she was glad. He was glad too. He still wanted to know what had happened. She had not told him what Natalia and Mikhail proposed, and he could not connect the attempt to their recovery without it. Asking again seemed likely to bring another household object at his head. Whatever Lynleit had planned, they had not completed it. The attempt and what followed had nevertheless changed them enough for the curse to lose its hold. He left the subject alone when they next met. She had prepared an answer. There was no occasion to use it. Lynleit,Kyrien,Natalia,Father Mikhail

entries.text: Doom Has an Address · Version 3 · Superseded Chapter 07 · Lynleit Disappears A shared curse sends Lynleit from Natalia's scholarship to Father Mikhail's blunt advice. After an incomplete attempt at intimacy, she has recovered but still has questions she refuses to discuss. Lynleit and Kyrien destroy a Holumn together and complete the final condition of its mechanism. The Holumn transfers one terminal curse across both identities, causing progressive physical decline and a prognosis measured first in weeks and then in days. Suppressing the curse in either person fails because the remaining attachment reconstructs it in the other. The traditional solution requires one of them to die first so the surviving identity is released. Lynleit rejects the fatal solution, consults other Magi, and searches Magiarchal records and prohibited theurgical procedures for an alternative. Natalia proposes that the curse recognizes the ego, quotes Jung's definition, and suggests reciprocal transformation as an alternative to death. Father Mikhail reaches the same conclusion through Church records and tells Lynleit that physical intimacy could work only if an existing attachment changes both identities. Lynleit withholds the proposed method from Kyrien and investigates their relationship as a possible procedure. Lynleit attempts to initiate an encounter but does not fully cross the boundary between them. The curse begins weakening the following morning and is later gone. Lynleit's unread pages and repeated denials suggest that she still wants Kyrien now that the curse is gone. inferred Kyrien knows about Lynleit's attempt, her refusal to explain it, and the curse's decline, but lacks enough information to connect them. The incomplete attempt and its aftermath change both identities enough for the curse to lose its hold. Doom Has an Address The condition The Holumn was eventually destroyed. That was the first mistake. Lynleit and Kyrien did not understand what they were fighting until after they had already killed it. Destroying the creature completed the final part of its mechanism: its own terminal condition passed to whoever had caused its death. They had destroyed it together. There was still only one curse, attached to both of them. Their bodies began to weaken. Sleep stopped restoring them properly, and minor injuries healed too slowly. Lynleit found her magecraft increasingly exhausting. Kyrien began stopping on stairs. Within days, ordinary exertion had become difficult for both of them. The Magi who examined the curse gave them several weeks. Attempts to suppress it produced a second discovery. Removing it from Lynleit brought relief only until the attachment to Kyrien restored it. Treating him produced the same result in reverse. One of them could survive if the other died first. Lynleit rejected the answer. She spoke to other Magi, searched Magiarchal records, and investigated prohibited theurgical procedures. Could memory erasure work? A coma? Destroying magical capacity? Every answer sent her back to the same choice. Having one of them declared dead would not help either. The curse had no interest in legal language. Eventually she called Natalia. The academically respectable answer Natalia was silent long enough that Lynleit checked the connection. "This is older than your Holumn," she said at last. "Not the creature itself. The mechanism. People have been inventing versions of it for thousands of years." Lynleit leaned back against the desk. "Such as?" "The Assyrians had a substitute-king ritual. If an omen predicted the king's death, they could install another man in his place and let the omen fall on him instead. The important part wasn't biology. It was identity. For the duration of the rite, that man occupied the position the omen recognized as king." "Comforting." "It gets worse. Japanese purification rites used human-shaped substitutes to receive pollution or misfortune from a person. Folklore is full of beings whose life is hidden somewhere outside their bodies. An egg, an animal, a box, a tree. Destroying the body does nothing because the actual point of attachment is elsewhere." Lynleit frowned. "You're saying the Holumn did the same thing." "Almost. It inverted the principle." Natalia's voice became more focused. "It hid its death in the people who killed it." Lynleit said nothing. "And then there is the old logic of sympathetic magic," Natalia continued. "Things that have been joined remain connected after separation. Hair, blood, possessions, names, vows. Primitive language for a phenomenon your Magi would dress up with considerably more mathematics." "So when Kyrien and I destroyed it together..." "You didn't each receive half a curse. That would be easier. You became two coordinates of the same one." Lynleit looked down at her hand. "If I suppress mine, his restores it." "Because the structure still resolves correctly. Kyrien exists. You exist. Both of you remain sufficiently identical to the people who performed the act. The curse checks its address and finds both occupants still at home." "Then the usual solution really is what they told me." "One dies first." The words settled badly between them. Lynleit stared out the window. "I'm not doing that." "I assumed as much." "There has to be another way." "There usually is. People just become lazy when death works reliably." Lynleit closed her eyes. "Natalia." "I'm serious." "Then explain." Another pause. "What exactly do you think the curse recognizes?" "Us." "No. Think." Lynleit exhaled through her nose. Natalia had used that tone in lectures too. "The people who killed it," she said. "And what makes you the same person now?" "I called you so you could answer questions, not sit me down for an examination." "Unfortunately, you've always needed both." "Natalia." "The ego," Natalia said. "That's where I would begin. Jung describes it as 'a complex of ideas which constitutes the centre of my field of consciousness.' Not the whole psyche. The conscious sense of identity. The part that says this is me, this happened to me, this is what I want, this is where I end and the rest of the world begins." Lynleit straightened slightly. Natalia continued. "If the curse attached itself to that structure, then biological death is merely the most absolute way of disrupting it. It isn't necessarily the only way." Lynleit was quiet now. "You think the ego can change enough that the curse stops recognizing it." "Exactly." "How much?" "That I don't know." "Helpful." "I can tell you what would not be enough. New clothes. A new title. Hypnosis. Memory tampering at the surface level. Pretending to become someone else. The change would have to reach the architecture beneath ordinary self-description." "What kind of change?" "The kind after which a person can truthfully say that the one who entered an event and the one who emerged from it are not psychologically identical." Lynleit looked toward the floor. "Trauma," Natalia said. "Religious conversion. Surviving something that forces a complete reorganization of one's values. Grief can do it. Parenthood sometimes does it. A genuine confrontation with death certainly can." "We already have one of those arranged." "Yes. I was hoping for something less terminal." Lynleit rubbed her forehead. "And you think both Kyrien and I would have to change?" "Most likely. The curse is relational. Altering one coordinate might destabilize it, but if the other remains intact it may simply reconstruct the original pattern. You need to damage the relation itself." "Damage?" "Change, if you prefer a nicer word." "Into what?" Natalia went quiet again. Lynleit knew that silence. It was the silence Natalia used immediately before saying something she knew would irritate her. "No." "I haven't said anything." "You were about to." "I was." "Natalia." "Fall in love." Lynleit stared at the phone. For several seconds neither spoke. Then Lynleit said, very carefully, "You cannot possibly be serious." "I am entirely serious." "You spent the last ten minutes explaining Assyrian death rituals, sympathetic magic, external souls and Carl Jung so that you could tell me to fall in love?" "When you phrase it like that, it does sound theatrical." "Natalia." "Love is one of the few ordinary human experiences capable of reorganizing identity at several levels simultaneously. Future, loyalty, fear, attachment, self-image, boundaries. People begin making decisions as though another person has partially entered the structure of the self." "That is sentimental nonsense." "No. Sentimental nonsense is what poets do with it afterward." Lynleit said nothing. "If the Holumn's curse is anchored to where each of you draws the boundary between self and other," Natalia continued, "then a sufficiently profound reciprocal attachment could distort that boundary enough to break the original configuration." "You make it sound like surgery." "At the moment, it is." "And how exactly do you prescribe falling in love with someone?" "You don't." "Then this is useless." "I didn't say it was convenient. You asked what might work." Lynleit closed her eyes. Natalia added, almost casually, "There are faster ways to produce similar changes, of course." Lynleit opened them again. "I dislike the way you said that." "You should." "What ways?" "Ask someone else." "Natalia." "I've already given you the academically respectable answer." "And the unrespectable one?" Natalia laughed softly. "Go speak to a priest." Lynleit eventually hung up with considerably more knowledge and considerably less dignity than she had possessed before making the call. The unrespectable answer She sought a second opinion. Then a third. Eventually the investigation took her to Father Mikhail. Unlike Natalia, Mikhail had access to older theological records concerning curses that attach themselves to personal identity rather than flesh or soul. His conclusion was disturbingly similar. The Church had encountered analogous phenomena before. Not identical curses, but conditions in which an entity remained attached to a person's psychic continuity. Conversion sometimes worked. Marriage occasionally worked. Surviving war sometimes worked. Parenthood had worked once. A profound confession followed by absolution had produced partial success in another case. None of these things were magical rituals in themselves. The common element was transformation. An old organization of the self ceased to be sufficient. Something new replaced it. Mikhail explained this patiently while Lynleit took notes. Then she reached the practical question. "What would you recommend for Kyrien and me?" Mikhail looked at her. Lynleit waited. The priest appeared to consider several centuries of theology. Then he said, completely straight-faced: "Just have sex, loser." Silence. Lynleit became red from her throat to her ears. "What?" "You heard me." "You are a priest." "An observant one." She stood. "Lynleit." She grabbed her coat. "There are theological reasons." She headed for the door. "Lynleit." She opened it. "Sex is not the important part." She stopped. Mikhail remained seated. "The important part is what happens when two people who have spent years maintaining separate identities voluntarily cross a boundary that neither can afterward pretend was never crossed." Lynleit slowly turned around. "If there is already sufficient attachment between you, physical intimacy may produce exactly the discontinuity you need. Body, trust, vulnerability, future expectation, shame, desire, identity. Several layers of the psyche move at once." "And if there isn't sufficient attachment?" "Then you will merely have had sex." Her expression became murderous. Mikhail shrugged. "Which is why I recommend choosing your partner carefully." She left. Only in the corridor did Lynleit realize that she had written SEX? in enormous letters across the middle of her notebook. She nearly tore the page out. An alternative She did not tell Kyrien. He knew the prognosis, the failed attempts at suppression, and that she was still searching. He did not know what Natalia had told her. He did not know what Mikhail had told her. Most importantly, he did not know that Lynleit had begun treating their relationship as a possible procedure. At first she refused the idea. Then she investigated it. Then she attempted to disprove it. The Church called it transformation. Natalia called it reorganization of the ego. An old Magiarchal text called it discontinuity of identity; a thaumaturgical paper, failure of sympathetic recognition. Every source she consulted gave her another reason to return to the page she had nearly torn out. Meanwhile, their remaining weeks became days. Two days later Natalia called two days later. "So." "No." "I haven't asked anything." "You were about to." "I was." Lynleit continued reading. Finally Natalia said, "How do you feel about Kyrien now?" "The same." "Really." "Yes." "Nothing changed." "Nothing relevant." "Interesting distinction." "There is no distinction." "Of course." Lynleit turned a page she had not read. Natalia waited again. "The curse is gone," Lynleit said. "It is." "Kyrien is alive." "He is." "I am alive." "Also true." "The intervention therefore accomplished its purpose." Natalia made a thoughtful sound. "It failed." "It worked." "By failing." Lynleit closed the book. "There will not be another attempt." "I didn't suggest one." "There is no reason for one." "Correct." "The matter is resolved." "Completely." Lynleit narrowed her eyes. Natalia said nothing. That silence was intolerable. "There is absolutely no reason whatsoever for Kyrien and me to repeat anything that happened that evening." "I agree." "Good." "Good." Another silence. Then Natalia asked: "Are you disappointed?" Lynleit hung up. She opened the book again. The page was unfamiliar. So was the one before it. There had been a reason for that evening. A reason she could write down, defend, and blame on someone else. Now the curse was gone. She put the notebook under the book and tried to read. Kyrien's account Kyrien understood considerably less. He knew Lynleit had tried to sleep with him while behaving as though she were attempting an assassination. He knew she refused to explain why. He knew the curse had begun weakening the following morning. Any mention of that evening made her hostile enough to weaponize household items. There was a connection between these facts. He was missing something. This irritated him. Lynleit intended to keep it that way. The incomplete attempt and what followed had changed both of them enough for the curse to lose its hold. It could no longer recognize the exact pair of identities that had destroyed the Holumn. They survived. As far as Lynleit was concerned, the boundary between them remained uncrossed. Mostly. Lynleit,Kyrien,Natalia,Father Mikhail

The Holumn transfers one terminal curse across both identities, causing progressive physical decline and a prognosis measured first in weeks and then in days. Suppressing the curse in either person fails because the remaining attachment reconstructs it in the other. The traditional solution requires one of them to die first so the surviving identity is released. Lynleit rejects the fatal solution, consults other Magi, and searches Magiarchal records and prohibited theurgical procedures for an alternative. Natalia uses a two-name diagram, her failed decision diary, and her experience after leaving the Academy to explain why a change of identity must go deeper than its description. She introduces the ego hypothesis and quotes Jung. Lynleit jokes with Natalia, works through the examples, and keeps the diagram; Natalia proposes reciprocal attachment as a possible change, not a guaranteed cure.
