She spoke to other Magi, searched Magiarchal records, and investigated prohibited theurgical procedures. Could memory erasure work? A coma? Destroying magical capacity? Every answer sent her back to the same choice. Having one of them declared dead would not help either. The curse had no interest in legal language. Eventually she called Natalia. The academically respectable answer Natalia was silent long enough that Lynleit checked the connection. "Natalia?" "I'm here. Find something to write on." Lynleit pulled a sheet out from under a report. "Should I put my name at the top?" "Twice, if it helps." "It rarely helped with your marking." "Two names, then. Yours and Kyrien's." Lynleit wrote them side by side. "Join them," Natalia said. "Now cross yours out." The pen stopped. "On the paper, Lynleit." "I know. I was enjoying the lesson." "If I gave that sheet to someone who knew Kyrien, could they still find you?" "Through him." "And if you crossed out his name instead?" "They could ask me." "There. Suppression rubs out part of the address. It leaves someone who can supply the missing part." Lynleit looked at the line between the names. She had drawn it through an old calculation. "So they keep treating us as separate patients." "Which is a sensible place to begin. Unfortunately, you have already tested it." "Several times." "And nearly exhausted yourselves proving the same thing. Keep that sheet. We're going to stop repeating it." Lynleit drew a small, unfriendly face beside her name. "This is older than your Holumn," Natalia continued. "The mechanism, I mean. People have been trying to move a death from one person to another for a very long time." "With results?" "The Assyrians had a substitute-king ritual. A fatal omen threatened the king, so another man occupied his place and received his fate." "Comforting." "The useful question is why the omen would accept the substitute. It wasn't looking for the king's face. It recognized a position someone else could occupy." "And ours recognizes the people who killed it." "Yes. Usually you hear stories about a creature hiding its life in an egg, or an animal, or a locked box. Killing the body doesn't finish the job." Lynleit turned the pen over. "This one hid its death in us." "Exactly." She stopped drawing. "Then the usual solution really is what they told me." "One dies first." The words settled badly between them. Lynleit stared out the window. "I'm not doing that." "I assumed as much." "There has to be another way." "There usually is. People just become lazy when death works reliably." Lynleit closed her eyes. "Natalia." "I'm serious." "Then explain. I'll even stop decorating your diagram." "What exactly do you think the curse recognizes?" "Us." "No. Think." Lynleit exhaled through her nose. Natalia had used that tone in lectures too. "The people who killed it," she said. "And what makes you the same person now?" "I called you so you could answer questions, not sit me down for an examination." "Unfortunately, you've always needed both." "Only because you refuse to send the answers." "The ego," Natalia said. "Jung describes it as 'a complex of ideas which constitutes the centre of my field of consciousness.' Put that down. Leave space underneath." "For the translation?" "For your objections. The ego isn't the whole mind. It's the part around which you arrange what you consciously call yours. Your decisions, your memories, your intentions. You can forget what you ate yesterday without ceasing to recognize yourself." "I haven't forgotten. I object to calling it food." "Then the memory is doing very well." Lynleit wrote the definition. "So the curse doesn't need every memory intact." "That would be my first objection to erasing them. You might lose a year and still make the same choices for the same reasons. We need to know what it would take for its old description of you to stop being enough." "Can you measure that?" "I once thought I could. I kept a notebook of my decisions for three weeks. Every choice, followed by the reason I thought I'd made it." "How many notebooks?" "Too many. I was very pleased with them." "Always a warning." "Eventually I noticed that the woman in the notebooks was wonderfully reasonable. She never ate because she was bored. Never postponed a letter because she disliked the recipient. She had excellent reasons for everything." "You should introduce us." "I couldn't. I'd made her up. By the time I wrote down a choice, I'd already tidied it." Lynleit smiled and pushed the reports aside. "What did you try instead?" "I wrote down what I expected to do before I did it. Then what actually happened, including the little things I wanted to leave out. Tea, letters, unfinished work. The two columns disagreed much more often." "And that worked?" "It showed me where to look. It didn't explain every disagreement. Some days I was simply tired." Lynleit divided the space below the quotation into two columns. "Expectation and result." "Yes. For you, that means a new description of yourself is not enough. Calling yourself fearless doesn't remove a fear. Losing a title doesn't necessarily change how you make a decision. Changing clothes certainly won't help." "A pity. I could have been cured before lunch." "You're still looking for a procedure you can complete without anything happening to you." "I'm prepared to be mildly inconvenienced." "Lynleit." She put the pen down. "How much has to change?" "That I don't know." "Helpful." "I can give you a difference you already understand. When I left the Academy, I took my books home and thought I would begin all the work I'd been postponing." "And did you?" "I spent the first morning drafting a request to conduct it." Lynleit laughed once, then pressed a hand against her ribs. "To whom?" "An excellent question. I had nowhere to send it." "You could have sent it to me. I'd have approved it." "You would have corrected my handwriting." "Both. I'm generous." "I had stopped being a professor on paper. I was still waiting for someone to permit the next experiment. That habit took longer to notice. Longer still to stop." Lynleit picked up the pen again. "So handing in your resignation wasn't the whole change." "No. Nor would taking the title away from me now put me back where I was. I have done the work. Made mistakes I couldn't assign to the Academy. Paid for them myself." "And you still give examinations over the phone." "Some habits are worth keeping." Lynleit looked at the two names. "Trauma could do it." "It can. So can a religious conversion, grief, parenthood. But none is a reliable instruction. Two people can survive the same event and make very different things of it." "We already have a confrontation with death arranged." "Yes. I was hoping for something less terminal." "And both Kyrien and I would have to change." "Most likely. Go back to your sheet. You crossed out one name and could still recover it through the other." "So changing only me leaves him holding the old answer." "That is the risk. Whatever happens has to change what each of you is to the other." "Into what?" Natalia went quiet again. Lynleit knew that silence. It was the silence Natalia used immediately before saying something she knew would irritate her. "No." "I haven't said anything." "You were about to." "I was." "Natalia." "Fall in love." Lynleit stared at the phone. For several seconds neither spoke. Then Lynleit said, very carefully, "You cannot possibly be serious." "I am entirely serious." "You gave me homework, introduced me to Carl Jung, and told me about a dead substitute king so that you could tell me to fall in love?" "When you phrase it like that, it does sound theatrical." "I was trying to make it sound expensive. I don't intend to pay." "Think about an ordinary evening. You're absorbed in something. Someone you care about was meant to call an hour ago. You read the same sentence three times. You decide to work for another ten minutes before checking your phone." "And check it after two." "Thirty seconds, in my case. Myka was quite safe. I'd spent an hour pretending I could concentrate while I waited to hear it." "You could have called her." "I did. She asked whether I needed help with something." "Did you?" "I needed her to stop sounding so pleased with herself." Lynleit glanced at her own phone. "All right. Someone matters to you. How does that become enough to save us?" "It may not. Worrying over a missed call isn't a cure. But notice how much of an ordinary evening can already depend on someone else's safety. Now imagine finding you can't make plans for your own future without making room for that person. Even plans you never intend to show them." "That is sentimental nonsense." "No. Sentimental nonsense is what poets do with it afterward." Lynleit said nothing. "You don't have to become agreeable," Natalia added. "You may be thoroughly annoyed. The question is whether you still make the same decisions about your life once theirs has become part of it." "And whether they do the same." "Yes. That's why I'm talking about a reciprocal change. One person longing beautifully while the other carries on as before is no help to my hypothesis." "You make it sound like surgery." "At the moment, it is." "And how exactly do you prescribe falling in love with someone?" "You don't." "Then this is useless." "I didn't say it was convenient. You asked what might work." Lynleit closed her eyes. Natalia added, almost casually, "There are faster ways to produce similar changes, of course." Lynleit opened them again. "I dislike the way you said that." "You should." "What ways?" "Ask someone else." "Natalia." "I've already given you the academically respectable answer." "And the unrespectable one?" Natalia laughed softly. "Go speak to a priest." "You're enjoying this far too much." "I'm enjoying speaking to you. I'd prefer you weren't dying." Lynleit's hand tightened around the pen. "Then keep your afternoon free. I'm going to bring you a very unreasonable objection." "I look forward to it." After the call, Lynleit copied the two names onto a clean page. Underneath she wrote: What would have to change in both? She folded Natalia's first diagram and kept it inside the notebook. The unrespectable answer She sought a second opinion. Then a third. Eventually the investigation took her to Father Mikhail. Unlike Natalia, Mikhail had access to older theological records concerning curses that attach themselves to personal identity rather than flesh or soul. His conclusion was disturbingly similar. The Church had encountered analogous phenomena before. Not identical curses, but conditions in which an entity remained attached to a person's psychic continuity. Conversion sometimes worked. Marriage occasionally worked. Surviving war sometimes worked. Parenthood had worked once. A profound confession followed by absolution had produced partial success in another case. None of these things were magical rituals in themselves. The common element was transformation. An old organization of the self ceased to be sufficient. Something new replaced it. Mikhail explained this patiently while Lynleit took notes. Then she reached the practical question. "What would you recommend for Kyrien and me?" Mikhail looked at her. Lynleit waited. The priest appeared to consider several centuries of theology. Then he said, completely straight-faced: "Just have sex, loser." Silence. Lynleit became red from her throat to her ears. "What?" "You heard me." "You are a priest." "An observant one." She stood. "Lynleit." She grabbed her coat. "There are theological reasons." She headed for the door. "Lynleit." She opened it. "Sex is not the important part." She stopped. Mikhail remained seated. "The important part is what happens when two people who have spent years maintaining separate identities voluntarily cross a boundary that neither can afterward pretend was never crossed." Lynleit slowly turned around. "If there is already sufficient attachment between you, physical intimacy may produce exactly the discontinuity you need. Body, trust, vulnerability, future expectation, shame, desire, identity. Several layers of the psyche move at once." "And if there isn't sufficient attachment?" "Then you will merely have had sex." Her expression became murderous. Mikhail shrugged. "Which is why I recommend choosing your partner carefully." She left. Only in the corridor did Lynleit realize that she had written SEX? in enormous letters across the middle of her notebook. She nearly tore the page out. An alternative She did not tell Kyrien. He knew the prognosis, the failed attempts at suppression, and that she was still searching. He did not know what Natalia had told her. He did not know what Mikhail had told her. Most importantly, he did not know that Lynleit had begun treating their relationship as a possible procedure. At first she refused the idea. Then she investigated it. Then she attempted to disprove it. The Church called it transformation. Natalia called it reorganization of the ego. An old Magiarchal text called it discontinuity of identity; a thaumaturgical paper, failure of sympathetic recognition. Every source she consulted gave her another reason to return to the page she had nearly torn out. Meanwhile, their remaining weeks became days. Two days later Natalia called two days later. "So." "No." "I haven't asked anything." "You were about to." "I was." Lynleit continued reading. Finally Natalia said, "How do you feel about Kyrien now?" "The same." "Really." "Yes." "Nothing changed." "Nothing relevant." "Interesting distinction." "There is no distinction." "Of course." Lynleit turned a page she had not read. Natalia waited again. "The curse is gone," Lynleit said. "It is." "Kyrien is alive." "He is." "I am alive." "Also true." "The intervention therefore accomplished its purpose." Natalia made a thoughtful sound. "It failed." "It worked." "By failing." Lynleit closed the book. "There will not be another attempt." "I didn't suggest one." "There is no reason for one." "Correct." "The matter is resolved." "Completely." Lynleit narrowed her eyes. Natalia said nothing. That silence was intolerable. "There is absolutely no reason whatsoever for Kyrien and me to repeat anything that happened that evening." "I agree." "Good." "Good." Another silence. Then Natalia asked: "Are you disappointed?" Lynleit hung up. She opened the book again. The page was unfamiliar. So was the one before it. There had been a reason for that evening. A reason she could write down, defend, and blame on someone else. Now the curse was gone. She put the notebook under the book and tried to read. Kyrien's account Kyrien understood considerably less. He knew Lynleit had tried to sleep with him while behaving as though she were attempting an assassination. He knew she refused to explain why. He knew the curse had begun weakening the following morning. Any mention of that evening made her hostile enough to weaponize household items. There was a connection between these facts. He was missing something. This irritated him. Lynleit intended to keep it that way. The incomplete attempt and what followed had changed both of them enough for the curse to lose its hold. It could no longer recognize the exact pair of identities that had destroyed the Holumn. They survived. As far as Lynleit was concerned, the boundary between them remained uncrossed. Mostly. Lynleit,Kyrien,Natalia,Father Mikhail

entries.title: The Empty Boats Beneath the Bridge
entries.subtitle: Chapter 05 · Unknowing Convergence
entries.text: The Empty Boats Beneath the Bridge Chapter 05 · Unknowing Convergence A covert MSF inspection of apparently unmanned river shipments collapses when the Drowned Choir attacks from below, leaving Kyrien to witness Lynleit's forbidden water walking from the quarantined bank. Sherie and Drake ask Lynleit to assemble a loyal team and inspect recurring night traffic on the Vilen river. Several surveillance nights produce no boats while small oddities emerge from the quarantined park. After the failed watches, Lynleit repeatedly challenges Kyrien to short card games and they learn each other's physical tells. Their unfinished rematches and attention to breath, hands, and pauses imply an attraction neither character names or allows to displace the operation. inferred Felix freezes the bridge cameras and remains on the city bank as fallback while Reiner leads Lynleit, Kyrien, Maren, and Ivo down onto the boats. When a boat shifts, Kyrien briefly steadies Lynleit near the concealed Sparrow holster and releases her before she asks. The empty boats, drowned hands, and pale girl imply that the contraband crews were taken before the interception. inferred Reiner, Maren, and Ivo reach the city bank with Felix's fallback line while Kyrien is forced toward the quarantined park bank. The drowned hands tear away Lynleit's blue suede jacket and drag her underwater until fury releases blue flame through the river. The river surface holds beneath Lynleit's palm, knee, and boots, allowing her to stand above hands that cannot cross it. The pale girl's silence and tilted head imply that Lynleit's survival contradicts the rule by which the Drowned Choir takes people. inferred Kyrien's careful denial and continued silence imply that he has chosen to protect Lynleit's forbidden ability before either of them openly trusts the other. inferred Lynleit crosses the held surface to the park bank and later sits back to back with Kyrien for warmth among the trees. Chapter 05: The Empty Boats Beneath the Bridge Working draft based on the confirmed river operation. Exact dialogue, further oddities during the unsuccessful watches, and the meaning of the girl's refusal to pursue Lynleit remain provisional. The Fifth Watch The bridge was closed at the park end. On the southern bank, a low riverside district faced the water through mature trees and garden fences. Old wooden villas stood beside modest masonry houses, their windows scattered across the slope. The nearest main road lay beyond them. Lamps threw pale circles across the pavement, and civil safety cameras watched the bridge from both approaches. On the northern bank, the same bridge ended at a locked path into the quarantined park. No lamps remained lit beyond the barrier. Trees had grown into a single black mass behind it. Drake's reports described small boats passing on the darkest nights, without navigation lights, visible cargo, or anyone at the controls. The timing looked deliberate. Contraband remained a possibility. Sherie and Drake had asked Lynleit for a team capable of observing the boats without turning the investigation into an official MSF operation. The plan was narrow. Felix would freeze the bridge cameras for as long as he could preserve a convincing loop, maintain communications, and remain on the city side as the fallback if the river team lost its exit. Reiner would secure the descent ropes. Lynleit, Reiner, Kyrien, Maren, and Ivo would board from above, inspect the boats, and leave by ropes at the next bridge. They were not to seize cargo, stop a suspect, or remain after the camera window closed. The first watch produced nothing. The second ended when Felix warned that the camera loop had begun to drift out of time with the traffic lights. On the third, a branch broke somewhere inside the park before the wind reached the trees. Kyrien turned toward the sound. Lynleit noticed him turning and looked as well. Neither said anything. On the fourth, one of the frozen camera feeds showed a pale interruption on the park path. Felix blamed compression damage. When he restored the live image, the path was empty. They had no authority to investigate the park, no safe way to extend the camera window, and no proof that either incident meant anything. Every night ended with the same order from Lynleit. "Restore the cameras. We leave." The second night had left Lynleit and Kyrien waiting inside the maintenance van while Felix restored the live feeds and Reiner recovered the anchors. Felix kept a worn deck of cards in a side compartment. Kyrien found it first. Lynleit sat opposite him. He won the first short game without speaking more than the rules required. "Again," she said. The rematch continued on the third night. Lynleit watched his hands until Kyrien asked whether she intended to look at her own cards. She did not answer. Before one reckless play, his breathing stopped for a beat. He won anyway. On the fourth night, she noticed the same pause and smiled before placing an ordinary card. Kyrien looked at her instead of the table. The hesitation was brief, but his next play was the safer one. "You changed the conditions," he said. "The cards are unchanged." He began watching her hands after that. By the end of the night, he had found the small movement of her thumb that came before a committed decision. They dealt another hand before the fifth camera window opened. Felix called them to position before either could finish it. Kyrien left his cards face down on the metal shelf. Lynleit left hers opposite them. By the fifth watch, nobody expected the boats. Felix sat inside a maintenance van on the city side with a compact terminal across his knees. The bridge cameras were displayed in four muted panes. Each showed a version of the previous several minutes with no MSF officers in it. "The loop is clean," he said through the earpieces. "Please do something before I have to put it back." Reiner tested the last anchor point with both hands. "Window." Felix gave him the remaining time. "Shorter than yesterday," Reiner said. "Yesterday had fewer buses. I was not consulted about the timetable." Lynleit stood against the inner rail and watched the black water below. She had chosen a fitted blue suede jacket instead of her usual coat because it would interfere less with ropes and wet timber. It still concealed the Sparrow carried above her tailbone, but did nothing against the cold rising from the river. The current caught fragments of city light and stretched them until they broke. Kyrien waited several paces away. He had no MSF insignia and no recognized place in the formation. Felix had assigned him no task that could not be watched by someone else. "If they do not appear tonight, we end the pattern," Lynleit said. "Because the operation has failed?" Kyrien asked. "Because repeating an intrusion after the target has noticed it is not surveillance." Felix looked up from the terminal. "That almost sounded directed at someone." Kyrien did not answer. Reiner lifted one hand. The bridge fell silent. Something had entered the far edge of the river. At first Lynleit saw only the interruption it made in the reflected lights. Then the first boat separated from the dark, followed by another and another. They were small, weathered wooden craft with dark tarps stretched across shallow holds. Their lamps were off. Fixed rudders kept their bows aligned while the current carried most of their weight toward the bridge. Nobody stood at the controls. Felix stared at the feed, then at the river itself. "Those are our boats." "I can see them," Reiner said. "There is nobody aboard." "That is what we are here to establish." Lynleit watched the distance close. "Positions." The officers moved. The Descent Reiner went over the rail first, paying out the rope in short, even lengths. Maren and Ivo followed on the adjacent line. Felix stayed with the terminal inside the locked maintenance van, watching the camera loop and every signal the descending team still transmitted. Kyrien waited until Lynleit reached the rail. "You first," he said. "Is that concern?" "If I go first, Felix may cut the rope." Felix's voice arrived through both earpieces. "The possibility has been evaluated." Lynleit swung over the side. The river moved beneath her boots. The lead boat passed under the bridge at the expected angle, steady enough that Reiner landed near its center without shifting its course. The others divided themselves between the following boats. Lynleit released the rope last and absorbed the impact through her knees. Kyrien landed behind her. His weight rolled the boat farther than Reiner's landing had. Lynleit's footing shifted on the wet boards. Kyrien caught her at the waist from behind. The heel of his hand met the leather edge of the Sparrow holster beneath her jacket. Lynleit's hand went to the rail instead of the pistol. Kyrien released her before she had recovered her balance completely. The boat continued forward. There was no pilot. There was no passenger. Lynleit pulled back the tarp. The hold was empty. No mechanism visible from the deck explained how the boat had kept its route beyond the fixed rudder and the current. Its shallow interior carried the practical alterations of a craft used to move things without inviting inspection. Tonight there was no cargo to inspect. Reiner's voice came from the first boat. "Empty." The second team confirmed the same. Felix opened the restricted channel. "Nothing in any of them? Check under the boards." Lynleit crouched beside the controls. The metal was wet. So was the deck. Nothing proved that a living person had occupied the boat recently. She looked back at the tarp. Someone had covered an empty hold. The park passed on their right. From the water, the trees appeared closer than they had from the bridge. Their lowest branches extended over the bank and hid the path behind them. Kyrien stopped breathing for one beat. Lynleit looked toward him before he turned to the trees. "What?" Lynleit asked. "Nothing." Maren shifted toward the gunwale. "There is something beside us." Reiner answered at once. "Do not lean out." She had already looked down. Her right leg vanished over the side. There was no splash large enough to explain the force. Her hip struck the gunwale, both hands caught the rail, and the rest of her body followed as if the river had taken hold of her boot. Reiner crossed from the lead boat before anyone else moved. He caught her wrist. For a moment his weight held her above the surface. Then his shoulder jerked downward. "Line," he ordered. Ivo threw it from the next boat and braced against a thwart. The boats had begun to separate, not quickly, but in different directions. The rope snapped tight between them. The woman in the water tried to kick toward the hull. Her face changed. "Something has my legs." Reiner pulled hard enough to bring her shoulder against the side. The water pulled harder. His footing broke, and he went in beside her. The river ceased to behave like water shared by bodies of different weight. It took each person according to a separate direction. Ivo entered to reach Reiner. Kyrien cut the slack before the line could take Lynleit with it, but the boat rolled beneath both of them. The gunwale struck her thigh. A moment later the deck was gone from under her feet. Cold closed around the team. Two Shores The city bank was the assigned emergency route. It had steps, lamps, and streets where an extraction vehicle could approach without crossing the quarantine. Reiner forced Maren toward it. When something pulled her legs down, he hooked an arm beneath her shoulders and kicked hard. Ivo reached them from the side. Together they gained a metre, lost half of it, and gained it again. Felix kept the communications channel open from the city bank. "City side. Do not fight for the boats. City side." The order gave the officers one direction when the river seemed determined to give each of them another. Hands caught at boots, ankles, and calves. Most of the officers felt only pressure and fingers where no person could remain submerged. They kicked free without seeing what they struck. Felix left the van only when the operation had already collapsed. He carried the fallback line down to the embankment steps and threw it toward the first heads he could distinguish. Reiner reached the wall and lifted Maren high enough for Felix to catch her from above. Ivo followed in fragments, coughing river water and helping pull Reiner beyond the edge. "It was hands," Maren said. Felix knelt beside her. "What was?" "On my legs. Someone was holding my legs." Reiner looked back at the river. Lynleit was not among them. Neither was Kyrien. The force beneath the water had turned Kyrien away from the city bank. He stopped spending strength on a direction the river would not permit and chose the nearer ground. The park bank offered mud, exposed roots, and a wall of unlit trees. He caught the lowest root with both hands and pulled himself out beneath the branches. The quarantine waited behind him. He remained low and moved inside the tree line. From there, he could see the broken formation of boats and the heads of the officers reaching the opposite shore. He could not see Lynleit. Then the river struck the underside of the surface from below. Beneath Lynleit knew how to swim. That knowledge survived for the first several seconds. She turned toward the nearest light, drove one arm forward, and tried to bring her legs behind her. Her right ankle stopped. Fingers closed around it. Another hand caught her calf. A third pressed against the back of her knee. They did not seize her in one direction. They climbed. She kicked and felt a wrist bend beneath her heel. The grip did not release. Her jacket dragged in the current and made every movement heavier. The surface was still visible. She could not reach it. Her fear of drowning had existed since childhood. Training had given it procedures: control the breath, identify the current, discard weight, choose a direction. The hands made each instruction useless. They were not a current. They did not tire. They had no single body against which leverage mattered. One closed around her other ankle. Others seized the suede jacket and pulled its hem over her hips, turning the fitted garment into another grip against her escape. The river pulled her farther from the light. She kicked again. The grip tightened. In the panic she wanted to hurt whatever was holding her, even if she had to turn and go deeper to reach it. Lynleit twisted downward instead of up. Blue flame broke from both hands and spread through the water without steam or loss of colour. It caught the drowned wrists as if the river were air. The hands burned beneath the surface. Fingers opened. Others caught at her sleeves, her boots, and the edge of the jacket until the suede tore free and disappeared among them. She tore upward through them. Her head broke the surface. Air entered as pain. She coughed, reached for anything that might hold her, and found nothing. Her palm struck the water and met resistance where her weight should have broken through. The surface bowed beneath her like stretched cloth, then held. Lynleit pressed down. She brought one knee onto the same impossible resistance, planted a boot, and pushed herself upright. Water ran from her ash-black hair across her face. Her breath would not slow. The river yielded by a few centimetres beneath each step but no longer admitted her body. Hands filled the darkness beneath her. Some were pale. Some had lost the shape of living hands. Small ones reached between larger ones. They opened and closed beneath the soles of her boots, pressing against the underside of the surface. None passed through it. Lynleit stood above them. From the trees, Kyrien watched without moving. The water ahead of Lynleit swelled. Hair appeared first, flattened against a white forehead. Then came a face with fishing line drawn through both eyelids. The knots were neat. Water dripped from them. The girl rose until the river released the upper half of her dress. Dead fish had been fastened together in overlapping rows, their bodies colourless, their mouths opening as the current passed through them. She faced Lynleit. The drowned hands continued reaching below. The girl said nothing. Lynleit could not tell whether sewn eyes were capable of looking at her, but she felt the attention settle. The girl's head tilted slowly to one side. Lynleit glanced down at her own boots, then back at the girl. She did not dare move yet. The Park Bank The girl did not pursue when Lynleit moved. Lynleit placed one foot before the other, testing the surface each time before trusting it. The water depressed beneath her boots and recovered behind them. She backed toward the park bank until mud and reeds replaced the impossible support beneath her feet. Kyrien found her beyond the lowest branches, where the bank rose into the trees. She had lost the blue suede jacket. Her blouse and the holster above her tailbone were soaked through, her ash-black hair clung to her cheeks and throat, and she was still breathing as if the hands remained around her legs. He removed his jacket. It was as wet as everything else and therefore useless. "A thoughtful gesture," Lynleit said. "I reconsidered it." "Sensibly." They moved deeper into the trees until the river could no longer be seen between the trunks. The city bank remained visible in pieces across the water. Felix and Reiner were gathering the officers beneath the bridge lights. On this side, the quarantine swallowed sound before it travelled far. Lynleit stopped at the base of a broad tree and sat. Kyrien lowered himself behind her. They settled back to back, shoulders touching through soaked clothes, each lending the other the little warmth that remained. For a while neither spoke. His breathing was slower than hers but not yet steady. Once, it stopped for the same brief interval she had learned across the cards. Lynleit looked across the river toward the officers gathering under Felix's light. "You came ashore on this side," Lynleit said. "It was closer." "So you could see the river." "Parts of it." She waited. "Did you see anything strange?" she asked. "The boats had no crews. Something tried to drown all of us. We are sitting inside a quarantined park in wet clothes." "That is not what I asked." "It is what happened." Lynleit turned her face slightly, not enough to look at him. "And nothing else?" "Nothing I can explain." Lynleit let her head rest back against his shoulder. "Then do not invent an explanation," she said. "I was not planning to." Across the river, Felix's light moved along the embankment. Reiner stood at the edge, looking toward the park. Kyrien saw the search before Lynleit did. He remained still for another moment, keeping his back against hers while her breathing slowed. Lynleit,Kyrien,Felix,Reiner,Sherie,Drake

entries.title: The Last Man Out
entries.subtitle: Chapter 02 · The Quarantine
entries.text: The Last Man Out Chapter 02 · The Quarantine Captain Heyk leads a specially equipped unit into Vilen's sealed park and becomes its sole survivor. Public disappearances force police to close the park before the government seals it even from them. Captain Heyk leads a specially equipped paramilitary unit into the park. Forces the unit cannot understand or explain massacre the squad. Heyk becomes the sole survivor and is evacuated by the Ducal Guard under Drake's orders. Grief for his squad follows him into a new role as a Ducal Guard field agent and bodyguard serving Drake and Sherie. Chapter 02: The Last Man Out Placeholder draft built from confirmed quarantine events. Exact action, dialogue, and the force inside the park remain undefined. The Public Cordon The park cannot be erased from public attention. Citizens vanish first. Private investigators and police officers disappear when they go looking for them. Families know who has not come home, and the absence of bodies makes every ordinary explanation less convincing. Police enforce the first quarantine to prevent more people from entering. Gas, poison, or another harmful substance remains possible, but no theory explains why nothing is recovered. Eventually the government seals the park even from the police. The Unit Captain Heyk enters with a specially equipped paramilitary unit tasked with investigating the park in full protective gear. They expect an environmental hazard, a criminal operation, or something else that training can name. The unit is massacred by forces Heyk cannot understand or explain. He becomes the sole survivor. The Evacuation The Ducal Guard removes Heyk from the park under Drake's orders. What warning reaches Drake, how the evacuation succeeds, and what follows Heyk out remain unresolved. Heyk survives with grief for the squad he lost and no language adequate to describe the cause. He is later recruited into the Ducal Guard as a field agent and bodyguard serving Drake and Sherie's interests. Heyk,Drake,Sherie

entries.title: The Name Left Behind
entries.subtitle: Chapter 04 · Unknowing Convergence
entries.text: The Name Left Behind Chapter 04 · Unknowing Convergence Natalia follows a missing name through the city archive and finds her niece Myka protecting the last surviving clue. Natalia finds a missing page hidden from every archive index. Myka reveals an unaltered copy carrying Fionn's name beside a future date. The archive erases the evidence while Natalia attempts to preserve it. Chapter 04: The Name Left Behind Placeholder draft. Replace this chapter when final story material is available. Missing Entry Natalia noticed the gap because the archive insisted there was none. A page number had been removed from every index, leaving the sequence perfect and the history incomplete. The missing name led her back to the Magi Academy, where her niece Myka had hidden the last unaltered copy inside a student spellbook. The Witness Fionn's name appeared in the margin beside a date that had not happened yet. Myka refused to explain how the record had been written. Someone entered the archive below them. The shelves began correcting themselves one book at a time. End Record Natalia photographed the page before it turned blank. The image preserved every word except the name she had come to find. Natalia,Myka,Fionn

entries.title: The Nameless Street
entries.subtitle: Chapter 06 · Divided Attention
entries.text: The Nameless Street Chapter 06 · Divided Attention Lynleit loses Felix during a walk after lunch and follows a child's cries through an impossible street. Lynleit and Felix take an ordinary walk through central Vilen after lunch. Lynleit finds herself alone, dizzy, and unable to navigate a street that does not obey the surrounding city. A little girl loses a red balloon and runs away crying. Lynleit catches the balloon and follows the girl's cries through the labyrinth. The girl leads Lynleit to a broken fence above the body of a dead boy, then pushes her from the ledge. Lynleit wakes on a city bench while Felix tries to revive her from an apparent fainting episode. The girl's smile and sudden push suggest that her crying was a lure. inferred Chapter 06: The Nameless Street Working draft based on the confirmed Nameless Street encounter. Exact dialogue, the route Lynleit and Felix take after lunch, and the sensory details of the street remain provisional. After Lunch Felix had spent most of lunch explaining why a senior officer's secure telephone was not secure. He continued after they left the restaurant, even though Lynleit had stopped answering him. "The problem," he said, "is that people confuse being important with being difficult to overhear." "You demonstrated this to him?" "I demonstrated it to myself. Telling him would have made him unhappy." "And not telling him?" "Keeps both of us happy." They walked without destination because neither had to return immediately. The older part of central Vilen rose and folded around them. Narrow streets bent between plastered facades and old brick. Timber gates opened into courtyards too deep to see from the road. Iron balconies hung above steep passages, and flights of stone steps connected streets built at different heights. A roof could appear level with the pavement on one side of a hill and three storeys below it on the other. He bought a folded newspaper from a street stall and carried it under one arm. Lynleit suspected he had no intention of reading it. They turned past a small square where children chased pigeons around a dry fountain. Felix said something about coffee. Lynleit did not hear the end of the sentence. The Street Without a Name She was alone. She looked back for Felix. The square was gone too. Lynleit stopped. Her head continued moving. The walls leaned and corrected themselves. A pressure behind her eyes made distance difficult to judge. She placed one hand against cold plaster and waited for the dizziness to settle. It did not. She had drunk no alcohol. Nobody at lunch had approached their table closely enough to drug her. She tested the thought twice because both conclusions felt remote, as though they belonged to someone reasoning in another room. "Felix?" Her voice travelled down the street and returned too softly. No answer came. There were no people at the windows. No voices behind the doors. No laundry moved above the courtyards. The street was not abandoned. Its doors were painted, its windows clean, and flowers stood in boxes beneath several sills. It appeared maintained by residents who had all agreed to leave a moment before she arrived. Lynleit began walking. The lane descended beneath an arch and opened onto a triangular courtyard. Three passages left it. She chose the widest one and emerged beside the same arch from the opposite direction. She returned to the courtyard and took the passage with stone steps. It climbed for longer than the hill could contain. At the top, the pavement sloped downward toward a row of doors whose numbers were not arranged in order. One bore a brass six. The next bore eighteen. The third had no number, only four empty holes where a plate had been removed. Lynleit tried to remember whether the old city had a street like this. She searched the corners of the buildings for a street sign. The headache sharpened. She heard a child crying. The Red Balloon A little girl stood at the far end of the lane. She wore a light coat buttoned to the throat. One hand held the string of a red balloon. Its color was the only clean color Lynleit had seen since losing Felix. The girl looked at her. For a moment neither moved. Then the string slipped from the girl's hand. The balloon rose slowly. Its thread dragged across the edge of a balcony, cleared the ironwork, and drifted down the street rather than into the open sky. The girl cried out and ran after it. She turned through a narrow passage and vanished. Lynleit reached for the thread as it passed. It caught across her fingers with almost no weight. "Wait." The girl did not return. Her crying continued somewhere beyond the passage. The passage narrowed until her shoulders almost touched both walls. It opened at the top of another stairway, then divided between a covered arcade and an alley descending beneath houses. The crying came from the arcade. She followed it. At the next turn the sound came from below. At the next, from behind her. The girl never appeared. Lynleit saw only the red balloon above her hand, brushing stone whenever the street bent too sharply. The thread gave her something straight to hold while the city refused every other direction. She crossed a small bridge between two buildings and found herself beneath it a minute later. She passed a blue door three times, although she never repeated a turn. A church tower appeared between the roofs, first ahead of her, then behind her, then close enough that she should have been able to touch its wall. No bell sounded from it. The crying weakened into broken breaths. "I have it," Lynleit called. "Stop running." Her own voice sounded intoxicated. She could no longer keep one shoulder from striking the walls. The headache pulsed with her steps, and the pavement rose under her feet at angles that made no physical sense. The Broken Fence The passage ended on a terrace above the lower city. An old fence ran along its edge. Several sections had been repaired with newer timber. One had broken outward and left an opening above a sudden drop. The girl stood there. She was no longer crying. She looked down through the broken fence with her hands resting at her sides. Lynleit approached carefully. The red balloon pulled upward behind her. "You should not stand there." The girl did not turn. Lynleit followed her gaze. A boy lay below. His body had come to rest against the base of a retaining wall. One arm was folded beneath him. His face was turned far enough away that Lynleit could not see it, but nothing in the angle of his neck belonged to a living child. Her hand opened. The red thread slid from her fingers. The balloon climbed above the terrace, passed the roofs, and became smaller against the colorless sky. Lynleit looked at the girl. The girl was smiling. Lynleit tried to step back. Her heel caught against the uneven pavement. The headache surged hard enough to empty the strength from her legs. The girl placed both hands against her. The broken fence passed beneath Lynleit's hands. Stone, roofs, and pale sky changed places. She saw the boy below growing larger. Then a white sheet struck her across the face. The Bench "Lynleit." The sheet struck her again. "If you are dead, this is going to become extremely inconvenient." She opened her eyes. Felix stood over her, violently fanning her with the folded newspaper. Behind him, the ordinary city moved without concern. People crossed the square. A bus braked somewhere beyond the buildings. The dry fountain was close enough for Lynleit to hear children running around it. She was lying across a bench. Felix stopped fanning. "There you are." Lynleit sat up too quickly and gripped the edge of the bench while the square tilted. "How long?" "Long enough for three strangers to decide I had murdered you and one to offer advice on reviving you." "Where did you find me?" Felix looked at the bench. "Here." "I mean before." His expression changed. The playfulness withdrew without leaving his face entirely. "You were beside me. Then you stopped answering. I thought you were ignoring me with unusual commitment." He crouched in front of her. "You took two steps toward the bench and collapsed." Lynleit looked past him. The old streets climbed behind the square exactly as they had before lunch. She could identify every entrance. None led toward the terrace, the blue door, or the silent church tower. No red balloon crossed the sky. Felix asked what she had seen. Lynleit pressed two fingers against the place behind her eyes where the pain was fading. "A street," she said. Felix waited. "Which street?" She looked at the folded newspaper in his hand, then at the city around them. "It did not have a name." The answer sounded less credible once spoken aloud. Felix did not laugh. entries.title: Drake: Biography
entries.subtitle: Official for Special Assignments
entries.text: Drake: Biography Official for Special Assignments Drake reaches the rank of State Councillor and serves as an Official for Special Assignments, an elite executive troubleshooter attached directly to a high-ranking personal office. Free from routine administration, he can carry delegated authority into confidential criminal inquiries, political counter-espionage, emergency audits, and diplomatic errands. His friendship with the Duke begins when Drake is the only official willing to tell him that he is wrong. The refusal to flatter earns a trust that later looks like pampering to hostile courtiers. He also trains his niece Sherie for diplomacy. He reads the park disappearances as cover for illegal material movement, but his peers ridicule the theory and the Duke remains skeptical. The Court's existing resentment makes his warning easier to dismiss as another indulgence granted to a favorite. Drake opposes Sherie's illegal approach to Lynleit and does not design its strategy. On a hill overlooking Vilen, his apprentice leads the negotiation while he speaks reluctantly. Drake refuses to hand sensitive evidence outside his circle and instead seeks selected MSF resources in exchange for concessions or favors. Drake identifies small boats travelling on the darkest nights without visible operators. He and Sherie arrange a covert inspection through Lynleit. The empty boats and the river attack force him to reconsider his explanation of the traffic. Connects disappearances and irregular movements to a suspected coup. Faces resentment over his friendship with the Duke. Reluctantly joins Sherie's approach to Lynleit. Asks MSF to investigate apparently unmanned river traffic. Drake

entries.text: Father Mikhail: Biography Church special envoy Mikhail is trained as a priest for public cover, a special envoy for restricted Church operations, and a field operative capable of confronting Magi. He becomes the first authority to discover that Lynleit has shared forbidden knowledge of magic with Kyrien, Felix, and Reiner. When she promises to contain the breach on her own terms, he warns that he may later be sent to clean up the consequences. During Arc 1, Mikhail travels to Cardiff on special-envoy duty. The assignment becomes a life-and-death ordeal in which he survives several Magi threats alone and defeats some of them. The Magiarchy and Church later send Lynleit to assist him. Their methods are morally incompatible, but they continue the mission and protect one another. The disagreement in Cardiff continues to affect Mikhail and Lynleit after they return to Narvea. His discovery of the witness breach also contributes to MSF taking on a Magi role under Church and Magiarchy oversight. Discovers Lynleit's disclosure to Kyrien, Felix, and Reiner. Travels abroad on special-envoy duty and faces several Magi threats. Receives her assistance at Church and Magiarchy request. Cooperates with Lynleit despite moral disagreement. Consults Church records about Lynleit and Kyrien's shared curse. Returns with a rift that affects his later dealings with Lynleit. Father Mikhail

entries.title: Felix: Biography
entries.subtitle: MSF officer, friend, and personal bodyguard
entries.text: Felix: Biography MSF officer, friend, and personal bodyguard Felix is Lynleit's long-standing friend and one of the MSF officers Fionn trusts as her personal bodyguards. He accompanies her on operations, official journeys, and casual outings. Lynleit reveals her secret recruitment of Kyrien only to Felix and Reiner. Felix regards Kyrien as a threat whenever the bodyguards are not close enough to protect her. He concedes only because Reiner chooses Lynleit's judgment, leaving Felix as the minority opinion. Felix never fully learns to trust Kyrien. Their recurring clashes turn protection into open friction, and Lynleit must reprimand Felix when his hostility interferes with the compartment she created. During an ordinary walk after lunch, he sees Lynleit collapse onto a city bench but never enters the Nameless Street she experiences while unconscious. Fionn's death, Lynleit's accusation, and the hunt for her arrest force Felix to decide whether loyalty means following the formal chain of command or protecting his friend. Kyrien later helps Lynleit contact Felix and Reiner from hiding, drawing them into her slow campaign to reclaim MSF from Helena. Serves alongside Lynleit as a friend and trusted bodyguard. Learns of Kyrien's secret recruitment. Accepts the arrangement without trusting Kyrien. Lends Lynleit his Rook after worrying about her Sparrow. Helps the hunted Lynleit reconnect with MSF. Felix

entries.title: Felix: Connections
entries.subtitle: MSF officer, friend, and personal bodyguard
entries.text: Felix: Connections MSF officer, friend, and personal bodyguard Lynleit Their bond is friendship as well as service. Felix can protect, question, tease, and accompany her with a familiarity that a mere subordinate would not possess, but that closeness also makes her secret trust in Kyrien difficult for him to accept. Kyrien Felix sees Kyrien as an unverified threat inside Lynleit's private circle. Being outvoted makes him tolerate the arrangement, not trust the man. Potential sexual tension Lynleit Established asymmetry Felix overt, Lynleit deflecting Lynleit is one of the few people his charm cannot simply move into the response he wants. Familiar affection, physical ease, and repeated deflection keep his attraction active even when he respects the boundary she has made. The tension is easy for readers to recognize because it already has a social rhythm: he advances through jokes and flirtation, she ignores or redirects him, and neither abandons the closeness underneath the exchange. It does not need to become a relationship to remain real. Potential sexual tension Sherie Emerging potential Mutual play, sincerity unresolved Sherie can match Felix's teasing without mistaking it for a complete confession. Her ability to see when he hides seriousness behind a joke gives him an opponent and possible partner who can enjoy the performance while still asking for something sincere. His unresolved feelings for Lynleit prevent Sherie from winning him by charm alone. Both use social ease as protection: Felix hides seriousness behind jokes, while Sherie hides vulnerability behind charm and diplomacy. Their chemistry is immediate, but similarity makes them capable of prolonged flirtation without honest movement. Sherie begins testing the friendship after learning that Lynleit has slept with Kyrien while still feeling responsible for Felix's affection. Her refusal to treat Felix as Lynleit's permanent responsibility creates a comic rivalry with Lynleit and a more serious test of whether Sherie wants Felix himself or only wants to win his attention. entries.title: Fionn: Biography
entries.subtitle: Magiarch and MSF founder
entries.text: Fionn: Biography Magiarch and MSF founder Fionn creates MSF with a public intelligence purpose and a hidden structure prepared for magical crisis. He embeds cryptology into ordinary behavior: blue clothing initiates recognition, followed by an innocuous conversational challenge-response known only to top officers he trusts. He refuses to declare one uncontested successor because naming an heir would paint a target on that person. Within his family, he is the virtuoso of a hereditary blue-flame magecraft defined by control and subtle application. The family house is also a discreet residential node for MSF, with offices and a library supporting selected work without replacing the formal headquarters in Turon. Foreign Magiarchates, church actors, criminal Magi, and Helena pursue incompatible objectives around Fionn. Their pressures converge without one actor commanding the complete assassination. Several individually rational reasons persuade Fionn to delay acting until reasonable caution becomes his fatal mistake. Fionn withholds the deepest parts of his life from Helena. He considers this protection; she considers it exclusion. His secrecy also leaves the people around him unable to compare what they know about the threats he faces. After his assassination, Lynleit and Kyrien must interpret his unfinished plans, concealed MSF signals, and the agendas of several enemies. His refusal to name one successor creates the succession crisis he hoped to prevent. Helena knowingly assists part of the plot, but neither she nor any other participant controls the full outcome. Directs MSF publicly and serves as Magiarch in secret. Prepares the agency for a magical crisis. Delays acting while several political and supernatural threats converge. Leaves concealed safeguards and no uncontested successor. Fionn

entries.title: Fionn: Connections
entries.subtitle: Magiarch and MSF founder
entries.text: Fionn: Connections Magiarch and MSF founder Lynleit His biological daughter and likely heir in practice, though he refuses to make any successor uncontested and leaves much of her inheritance unexplained. Converging agendas Criminal Magi, rival Magiarchates, church actors, and Helena may each enable a different part of the outcome without sharing one command structure or objective. Potential sexual tension Helena Established marriage Mutual, damaged by exclusion Fionn's affection and desire for Helena are genuine. He separates bodily and domestic closeness from the secrets he believes he must carry alone, never understanding that this division changes what their intimacy means to her. Their sexual tension survives inside a real marriage because attraction and grievance occupy the same private space. The closer they become physically, the harder it is for Helena to accept that Fionn still decides which parts of himself she is permitted to know. Fionn

entries.title: Fionn: Magecraft
entries.subtitle: Magiarch and MSF founder
entries.text: Fionn: Magecraft Magiarch and MSF founder Hereditary magecraft Blue flame Fionn carries the same lineage-bound blue flame later inherited by Lynleit. The flame is a family discipline with a broad range of applications. Practiced method Precision before volume His distinction is virtuosity. Fionn can shape the flame through subtle, controlled applications that Lynleit has not learned to reproduce. Generational contrast Control and force Fionn represents the refined expression of the lineage. Lynleit possesses less finesse, but a greater willingness to manifest the flame at an unsafe scale. Irreplaceable force Beyond ordinary weapons The lineage becomes essential against threats that firearms cannot resolve: immortal or rapidly regenerating Holumns, bodies that move without being alive, and barriers that ordinary force cannot break. Fionn

entries.title: Helena: Biography
entries.subtitle: Political usurper
entries.text: Helena: Biography Political usurper Fionn respects Helena's intelligence but withholds the deepest parts of his life. He believes he is protecting the family; she experiences the secrecy as exclusion from their marriage. She questions his schedules, visitors, trusted officers, and Lynleit's movements, without discovering all of his private protocols. Helena knowingly assists part of the pressure against Fionn without controlling the whole conspiracy. After his assassination she takes control of MSF, names Lynleit as the suspect, and orders her arrest. Her authority depends on keeping the accusation intact while the investigation exposes layers of conspiracy that extend beyond her own knowledge and seizure of MSF. She knows neither the blue initiation signal nor the conversational challenge-response that authenticates it among Fionn's trusted officers. Fionn's conservative old officers notice that Helena does not know his private recognition protocol. Their loyalty to his instructions begins undermining her command. Studies Fionn's movements and loyalties. Assists part of the conspiracy against him. Seizes MSF and directs the hunt for Lynleit. Fionn's old officers question her ignorance of his private protocol. entries.title: Heyk: Biography
entries.subtitle: Ducal Guard field agent and bodyguard
entries.text: Heyk: Biography Ducal Guard field agent and bodyguard Captain Heyk enters the park at the head of a specially equipped paramilitary unit, expecting a material threat that disciplined preparation can survive. Forces he cannot understand or explain massacre his squad. Heyk becomes the sole survivor and is briefly evacuated by the Ducal Guard under Drake's orders. Grief for the unit he lost becomes his primary motive. His survival also leaves him carrying an account that official language cannot make coherent. Heyk is recruited into the Ducal Guard as a field agent and bodyguard, serving Drake and Sherie's interests while remaining personally bound to the unanswered deaths inside the park. Leads a specially equipped paramilitary unit. Survives the massacre of his squad. Is evacuated by the Ducal Guard under Drake's orders. Enters Drake and Sherie's service. Heyk

entries.title: Hiyu: Biography
entries.subtitle: Criminology student and intuitive investigator
entries.text: Hiyu: Biography Criminology student and intuitive investigator Hiyu studies criminology with Yulia, but his reputation comes from personal investigations instead of class rank. She masters the established discipline. He follows loose fragments, invents methods on the spot, and pursues possibilities that initially sound ridiculous. Their constant friction gradually becomes a working dependency. From the public fragments surrounding the disappearances, Hiyu suspects that magic may be involved. He has no hidden knowledge and does not know magic exists. The hypothesis fits his intuitive pattern strongly enough that he decides to enter the quarantined park for evidence, pulling a reluctant Yulia into the attempt. His hunch is directionally correct, but gives him no practical understanding of Holumns, the Spill, or survival inside the park. The conviction that lets him challenge an accepted explanation also puts both students in physical danger. Hiyu and Yulia become increasingly dependent on their different methods. He remains largely unaware that their need for one another is developing romantic weight. Survival must teach him that a correct idea can still be incomplete and dangerous. Suspects magic despite not knowing it exists. Persuades Yulia to enter the quarantined park. Finds more danger than his theory prepared him for. Keeps seeking Yulia's criticism without recognizing his attachment. Hiyu

entries.title: Hiyu: Connections
entries.subtitle: Criminology student and intuitive investigator
entries.text: Hiyu: Connections Criminology student and intuitive investigator Yulia The procedural counterweight he complains around, relies upon constantly, and gradually becomes unable to investigate without. He does not recognize the emotional meaning of that dependence. Calibration His mind is excellent at opening possibilities and poor at deciding how much confidence, danger, or action a partial pattern deserves. Potential sexual tension Yulia Emerging arc Mutual, unequally conscious Yulia is the critic whose resistance makes an idea worth pursuing. He becomes dependent on her attention before he understands that the dependence is personal, leaving him oblivious to tension that is already changing how he seeks her out. Their arguments repeatedly force proximity and attention. They lean over the same evidence, reach for the same document, and forget ordinary distance while trying to prove incompatible explanations. Yulia notices first and steps away; Hiyu continues the theory and wonders why she moved. Her anger becomes disproportionate when his recklessness makes the possibility of losing him real. Hiyu recognizes the bond through absence: an investigation without her corrections becomes less interesting, and he keeps turning toward the place where she should be. Yulia and Hiyu become intimate by learning to communicate through the noise they already create together. Hiyu

entries.title: Hiyu: Strengths and weaknesses
entries.subtitle: Criminology student and intuitive investigator
entries.text: Hiyu: Strengths and weaknesses Criminology student and intuitive investigator Hiyu is driven by possibility, contradiction, and the pleasure of making an unlikely pattern click. He constantly experiences eureka moments, builds protocols while using them, and abandons a clean path as soon as a stranger one becomes interesting. He has a reputation for ignoring women because ideas consume his attention so completely. This also leaves him oblivious to the romantic tension slowly forming with Yulia. Divergent inference He can connect fragments through possibilities other investigators reject too early, which is how a non-Magus with no knowledge of magic nevertheless suspects it. Improvised method Hiyu invents investigative procedures in response to the problem in front of him, making him flexible where Yulia is disciplined and unreliable where she is exact. Dangerous conviction A brilliant possibility becomes a plan before he has established whether the environment is survivable. Partial success makes him even more reckless. ENTP strong Ne Confirmed Hiyu

entries.title: Hiyu: Tradecraft
entries.subtitle: Criminology student and intuitive investigator
entries.text: Hiyu: Tradecraft Criminology student and intuitive investigator Investigative strength Generative hypothesis Hiyu produces explanations from weak signals and follows intuitive threads far beyond what academic consensus would permit. Independent practice Personal investigations His strongest work occurs outside the classroom, where he can pursue an anomaly without waiting for permission or adapting it to an assigned method. Failure condition Insight without calibration Correctly suspecting magic does not teach him what magic can do, how to gather evidence safely, or when an unexplained environment has already outmatched him. Hiyu

entries.text: Inspector Leo: Biography Police inspector Leo is a married police inspector who trusts patient interviews and the belief that every disappearance leaves a human trail. Searchers vanish after entering the park, then the case is removed from police control under a government quarantine. Following procedure now means abandoning the investigation, while continuing it means challenging his own institution. He remains outside the hidden world of Magi and interprets the crisis through police evidence. The Church and MSF each know more than they admit, leaving Leo to investigate the authorities controlling the answers without understanding the supernatural order behind them. Investigates disappearances. Loses searchers sent into the park. Is excluded when the government takes over the quarantine. Questions the authorities withholding information. Inspector Leo

entries.title: Kyrien: Biography
entries.subtitle: Independent operator and later MSF director
entries.text: Kyrien: Biography Independent operator and later MSF director Kyrien begins the story as an independent figure and the son of a Narvean military commanding officer. His father introduces him to weapons and officer conduct unusually early. At five, Kyrien is allowed to hold a Sparrow and immediately aims it at a civilian in the street. His father stops and scolds him, making clear that familiarity with a weapon never permits a breach of protocol. The incident leaves Kyrien with a quiet affinity for military practice and the moral burden attached to force. After his father's death, he retains that mentality alongside access to surviving contacts, suppliers, knowledge, and tools. The inheritance later enables his attempt on a politician involved in causing his father's death. The target is under MSF protection. The attempt fails because the politician belongs to the Magi world, and Kyrien never learns that Lynleit was present and almost harmed by his actions. After the failed assassination, Lynleit takes over Kyrien's interrogation at a police office. An extraordinary transfer clause in MSF's government contract lets her offer conditional freedom in exchange for his service. He cannot explain the personal edge in her questions. She keeps his recruitment from Fionn and eventually tells only Felix and Reiner. Felix clashes with Kyrien; Reiner remains watchful but accepts Lynleit's decision. During the failed river watches, Kyrien plays cards with her and begins learning her tells. He later witnesses her water walking and keeps it secret. When Mikhail questions her about the breach, however, Kyrien tells him that Felix and Reiner also know. While Lynleit is in Cardiff, Kyrien protects Myka undercover at the Academy, relying on Felix and Reiner until Natalia intervenes. After Fionn's death he shelters Lynleit and helps her reconnect with the officers. Asked why he keeps risking his life without a reward, he answers: "Because there's a battle to be fought." Kyrien stays with Lynleit after she loses the authority to compel him. They survive a shared curse following an incomplete attempt at intimacy, but she will not explain the proposed treatment. Their sexual relationship begins later in Arc 1. When Lynleit inherits the Magiarchate and then disappears, Kyrien becomes director of MSF. He must manage its government contracts, divided loyalties, ordinary intelligence work, and response to the Spill without her magical authority. He does not know that they have a son. Retains his father's military contacts and attempts to kill the politician implicated in his death. Accepts Lynleit's offer of conditional freedom. Tells Lynleit that a battle is reason enough to fight. Protects Myka until Natalia can intervene. Survives the curse but does not learn why Lynleit attempted intimacy. Takes over MSF while Lynleit is absent. Remains unaware that Lynleit bore his son. Kyrien

entries.title: Kyrien: Conflicts
entries.subtitle: Independent operator and later MSF director
entries.text: Kyrien: Conflicts Independent operator and later MSF director Concealed recruit Felix distrusts him, and his position initially depends on Lynleit's protection. Command without a Magiarch He later runs MSF's ordinary and supernatural work while Lynleit is absent. Kyrien

entries.title: Kyrien: Connections
entries.subtitle: Independent operator and later MSF director
entries.text: Kyrien: Connections Independent operator and later MSF director Lynleit Handler and eventual partner She questions him knowing that his failed attack nearly harmed her, a fact he never learns. Their repeated card games create a voluntary contest inside the coerced arrangement. He later protects her water-walking secret, gives her refuge, and chooses to remain once her authority can no longer compel him. Near the end of Arc 1, one curse binds their identities after they destroy a Holumn together. Lynleit attempts intimacy without revealing the proposed treatment. The incomplete attempt is followed by recovery, leaving Kyrien with questions she will not answer. Kyrien's father Formative authority A military commanding officer who introduces Kyrien to weapons, protocol, and officer morality. His correction of Kyrien's first reckless act with a Sparrow becomes the foundation of his son's belief that using force also means accepting reciprocal danger. Myka Undercover charge Kyrien keeps Myka safe inside the Magi Academy through conventional field skills and contact with Felix and Reiner until Natalia reaches them. Lynleit Lynleit recruits him under threat of imprisonment. He later chooses to stay, keeps her forbidden ability secret, and gives her refuge. After their shared curse ends, she refuses to explain why she tried to sleep with him. He suspects a connection between the attempt and their recovery. Tien Tien serves Helena as a concealed assassin. Kyrien must contend with an opponent who also relies on deception and surprise. Potential sexual tension Lynleit Established arc Mutual, slow to surface Kyrien wants to beat Lynleit at cards and dislikes finding that she can read him. Her elegance and nerve also attract him. He stays because he wants the battle, then finds himself facing private questions that her orders cannot answer. After the attempted intimacy, she will not tell him why their curse disappeared. The interrogation, card games, protected secret, and voluntary decision to stay give this pairing different kinds of familiarity. In Doom Has an Address, an incomplete attempt at intimacy breaks the shared curse. Lynleit loses the excuse of treatment without losing her interest in Kyrien; he is left trying to understand what happened. Their sexual relationship begins later in Arc 1. Potential sexual tension Sherie Strong potential Situational and confrontational Sherie's charm is too deliberate to disarm him, but the precision behind it earns his attention. He is more likely to watch for the moment her performance fails than reward the performance itself. Sherie uses language and calibrated flirtation to control the rhythm of an exchange. Kyrien answers with silence, literalism, or no usable reaction at all. Repeated negotiation could turn her professional frustration into sexual tension without making them compatible or displacing Kyrien's eventual relationship with Lynleit. Kyrien

entries.title: Kyrien: Motivations
entries.subtitle: Independent operator and later MSF director
entries.text: Kyrien: Motivations Independent operator and later MSF director Survive Lynleit's control, master the intelligence side of MSF, face the Magus politician tied to his father's death, and eventually make choices inside the hidden world on terms that are genuinely his own. Kyrien

entries.title: Kyrien: Strengths and weaknesses
entries.subtitle: Independent operator and later MSF director
entries.text: Kyrien: Strengths and weaknesses Independent operator and later MSF director Kyrien speaks little, rarely smiles, and wants to win. Cards, chess, and a gunfight can all provoke the same stubbornness. He reacts quickly to cheating, sometimes at the expense of the safer objective. He watches people's habits closely and asks blunt questions when they change. Intelligence tradecraft 97 He turns surveillance, deception, logistics, human behavior, and escape planning into a substitute for magical perception. Strategic adaptation 94 His practical reasoning converts unfamiliar threats into usable procedures, leverage, and decisions that survive contact with reality. Survival discipline 92 He does not try to overpower Magi. He stays difficult to locate, corner, deceive, or kill. ISTP / INTJ Ti or Ni; ISTP lean Provisional Kyrien

entries.title: Kyrien: Tradecraft
entries.subtitle: Independent operator and later MSF director
entries.text: Kyrien: Tradecraft Independent operator and later MSF director Concealment Subterfuge Controls what others can infer about his intent, identity, loyalties, and next movement. He survives by giving opponents a convincing answer that is not the true one. Escape discipline Evasion Breaks surveillance, avoids magical attention, plans exits before entry, and refuses confrontations whose terms were chosen by somebody else. Misdirection Trickery Uses false patterns, staged weaknesses, timing, and selective truth to make stronger opponents commit to the wrong interpretation. Relative strength Obstacle movement His strength is most effective against his own body weight. He may not strike with the greatest force, but he moves quickly through difficult ground, pulls himself over obstacles, and can climb fences or walls when an escape route demands it. Preparedness Redundant options Kyrien usually keeps at least two objects available that are weapons or can become weapons. The pair changes with circumstance and may include a knife, keys, a pen, or a pocket pistol. The habit keeps options within reach rather than imposing a fixed loadout. Reciprocal force Firearms His father taught him that pointing a weapon creates an obligation. Kyrien keeps the lesson as a personal rule: "You cannot do much in this world without life or death stakes. But if you dare to point a gun at someone, you should be prepared to be shot yourself." He uses firearms to create distance, interrupt an attack, or open an escape route. Mobility Motorcycle The only driving licence he ever wanted was for a motorcycle. He values the machine as a narrow, responsive escape tool that is harder to trap than a car, not as a leisure accessory. Last resort Survival combat Fights to remain mobile and alive, combining practical close combat with terrain awareness instead of pursuing elegant or decisive victories. Leadership peak Intelligence operations His unofficial MSF association gives him access to surveillance, counterintelligence, field planning, and institutional command. By Lynleit's disappearance, this becomes the side of MSF he has mastered completely. Kyrien

entries.title: Lester: Biography
entries.subtitle: Demiholumn and Natalia's outside ally
entries.text: Lester: Biography Demiholumn and Natalia's outside ally Lester is a demiholumn, half human and half Holumn. The circumstances of his birth or transformation, and whether either description is fully accurate, remain unknown. He becomes Natalia's ally without becoming her employee. When one of her cases reaches an impossible barrier, his unusual nature can provide an answer that neither ordinary investigation nor conventional magecraft could reach. Lester's unusual abilities help Natalia with otherwise impossible cases. He also pushes back against her habit of examining him and notices when her attention becomes personal. His working relationship with Natalia develops sexual tension. His origins and the limits of his abilities remain unknown. Lives as a demiholumn whose origin is unknown. Helps Natalia without joining her business. Uses his unusual nature when her casework meets an impossible obstacle. Remains beyond the classifications used by hidden-world institutions. Lester

entries.subtitle: Demiholumn and Natalia's outside ally
entries.text: Lester: Conflicts Demiholumn and Natalia's outside ally Classification Institutions may treat his demiholumn nature as a threat rather than accept him as a person. Lester

entries.title: Lester: Connections
entries.subtitle: Demiholumn and Natalia's outside ally
entries.text: Lester: Connections Demiholumn and Natalia's outside ally Natalia Natalia is his trusted investigator ally, not his employer. She calls on him when a case crosses the boundary between difficult and impossible. Their attraction grows through his refusal to remain only an object of her analysis and her increasing ability to see the man without ignoring the demiholumn condition. Classification Any institution that reduces him to either a human witness or a Holumn threat will misunderstand what he is and may decide that he cannot be allowed to remain free. Potential sexual tension Natalia Established tension Mutual, differently expressed Natalia's analytical distance gives Lester something unusually difficult to provoke. He enjoys forcing the reserved researcher into immediate experience, but the tension changes when he wants her attention to recognize the man rather than examine the demiholumn condition. Repeated cases bring Natalia's examination of Lester into conflict with his insistence on being treated as more than a case. He provokes her to act; she notices more than he expected. Their attraction does not answer her questions about his demiholumn nature. Lester
