entries.title: Hidden World Foundation
entries.subtitle: World Foundation
entries.text: Hidden World Foundation World Foundation A direct guide to magic, Holumns, identity-bound curses, Lester's unresolved demiholumn nature, hidden history, political balance, and the setting's central conflict. Hidden World Foundation Magic Comes From Inside Reality Magic exists within reality. Psyche and soul are part of the world's structure, and their pressure becomes strongest wherever many lives overlap, especially in cities. Magi perceive weak points created by that pressure. They use conditions that reality can already support and push them toward a chosen result. That practice is lawful magecraft. Miracle-making belongs to a separate and forbidden category: acts that resemble wizardry or imitate sacred deeds associated with Jesus, saints, saviours, and other religious figures. The Church can condemn such an act even when its immediate effect appears harmless. When Nightmares Enter Reality A city can only absorb so much fear, memory, and psychic strain. Once the pressure becomes too high, nightmares stop being private. They cross into reality as manifestations called Holumns. There is no standard monster and no requirement that a Holumn possess a body. A manifestation may be a creature, weather or water behaving impossibly, a repeating event, a disembodied will, or a curse attached to a person, object, place, or action. Its rule carries the fear, memory, fixation, or fracture that gave it pressure. Containment always has a cost. Every intervention changes the balance. Suppressing one breach can move the pressure somewhere else, while destroying a visible form may leave the rule behind. In Doom Has an Address (HI-006), destroying the Holumn activates its fatal curse. Lynleit and Kyrien destroy one manifestation together and inherit a single terminal curse distributed across both identities. Suppressing the condition in either person causes it to reconstruct from the other. The curse breaks only after both people undergo a reciprocal change deep enough that its original identification of them no longer holds. A Demiholumn Exists Lester is a demiholumn, half human and half Holumn. His existence does not yet have a complete explanation. It is unclear whether he was born this way, became this way, or requires a different account entirely. Lester acts as Natalia's trusted outside ally. His part-Holumn nature sometimes lets him accomplish what should be impossible through ordinary investigation or conventional magecraft. The limits, cost, and institutional consequences of that nature remain unresolved. Why Magic Stayed Hidden Magi preserved their existence by remaining hidden. They contained supernatural problems, restricted their own activity, and prevented most people from learning that they existed. Eventually they split. Some accepted an uneasy partnership with the Church. Others refused and followed their own goals. The Magiarchy and its regional Magiarchates grew from that divide, giving Church-aligned Magi a structure that could be governed, watched, and understood politically. Those outside the sanctioned order became renegades and enemies of both the Church and the Magiarchates. Divided Authority No single institution controls the hidden world. The Church, the Magiarchy, state authorities, aristocratic families, and intelligence networks depend on one another and remain mutually suspicious. The Church and Magiarchy cooperate in containment while disputing the limits of each other's authority. Public Ignorance The Magi identify, contain, and erase breaches before the public can understand what it has seen. The Church knows the nightmares are real, knows the Magi can oppose them, and is wary of both. Most people do not know that magic exists. Institutions conceal incidents and suppress the evidence that might make the hidden world publicly credible. The institutions responsible for secrecy place social stability above public access to the truth. Under pressure, they may harden their rules, divide internally, or change their methods to survive. Suppression Doctrine The Church and the Magiarchy share responsibility for suppression doctrine. It exists to keep knowledge of magic from spreading through ordinary society, but the Church holds final sanction over its use. Magiarchal resources may investigate, contain, absorb, or remove witnesses under that authority. The doctrine does not prescribe one automatic punishment. The response depends on the witness, the credibility of their account, the scale of exposure, and the danger of leaving them outside institutional control. Possible responses include murder, assassination, or kidnapping; extortion, intimidation, or bribery; framing the witness as mentally ill; forced integration into Church staff or clergy; and forced integration into Magiarchy service staff or a comparable supervised role. Officials weigh secrecy, risk, and moral cost in each case. The First Missing Person The first missing person causes the Spill. Other factions exploit the crisis he creates. His identity and the circumstances of the breach remain unresolved. The disappearances that follow are caused by Holumns. This remains hidden behind missing-person cases, failed searches, and material explanations until the supernatural pattern becomes impossible to ignore. The unresolved moral boundary lies between containment and murder. Officials may absorb, discredit, coerce, or kill a witness under the same doctrine. World Archive

entries.title: Holumn Incidents and Victim Testimonies
entries.subtitle: Holumn Archive
entries.text: Holumn Incidents and Victim Testimonies Holumn Archive Victim testimony and incident evidence for physical, environmental, event-bound, disembodied, and curse-bound Holumn manifestations, including the shared terminal curse in Doom Has an Address. Holumn Incidents and Victim Testimonies This archive preserves accounts of Holumn contact as they are known across several institutions. Police and government records usually begin with material explanations. Magi and Church special envoys examine the same evidence for a governing supernatural rule. Forms and countermeasures are collected in Holumns. Accounts quoted below are testimony; the surrounding text records events and institutional interpretations. The Voice on the Line Record: HI-001 Known form: Disembodied will Primary medium: Telephone call and borrowed voice Have you heard of a telephone call that answers to you in your own voice? At first I thought whoever was on the phone was repeating me. But it was my own voice. At first it felt like an echo, because all it did was repeat my words. Then it started calling me incessantly, and it was talking to me in bizarre ways. In my own voice. Institutional readings Police and government Harassment, a compromised line, manipulated audio, or a distressed witness. Magi and special envoys A reflection that has crossed into agency. The voice no longer requires the witness to speak first. The Last Piece Record: HI-002 Known form: Attached curse Primary medium: A puzzle sold at a market The purchaser becomes increasingly compelled to solve the puzzle. Once the final piece is placed, the purchaser disappears and is entered into the missing-person system. No surviving victim testimony is known. Institutional readings Police and government A cluster of missing-person cases associated with an unverified market purchase. Magi and special envoys The object carries a condition. The disappearance occurs when the puzzle is completed. The Drowned Choir Record: HI-003 Known forms: Embodied and environmental manifestation Primary medium: The city river, drowned souls, and a humanlike body A pale girl emerges from the water. Her eyes are sewn shut with fishing line, and her dress is made from dead fish. The souls of people drowned in the river across generations are bound to her. Their submerged hands seize swimmers and pull them downward, and their voices form the choir through which she can speak. It felt as though my legs were being grabbed and pulled by someone's hands. Source: MSF Officer Maren after reaching shore The encounter occurs during a covert MSF operation requested by Sherie and Drake. Small wooden boats owned by contraband gangs move on the darkest nights without visible operators. Dark tarps cover their shallow holds, fixed rudders hold their heading, and the current provides most of their movement. Felix freezes the bridge cameras and remains on the city side as communications fallback while Lynleit, Reiner, Kyrien, Maren, and Ivo descend. When they pull back the tarps, the holds are empty. The Drowned Choir has already taken every crew before the boats reach the interception point. The officers are trained swimmers, but unseen hands make the short escape to shore nearly impossible. Reiner, Maren, and Ivo reach the street-facing city bank with Felix's fallback line. Kyrien is driven toward the quarantined park bank instead and observes the river from inside the trees. Only Lynleit sees the hands clearly after she is pulled underwater. They tear away the fitted blue suede jacket she chose for the operation. Fear and fury release her blue flame at full force. It burns the drowned hands beneath the water until their grip opens. When Lynleit breaks the surface, her palm meets resistance. She brings one knee and then both boots onto the same yielding layer. The river bows beneath her weight without admitting her body. Once she stands, the hands cannot cross the surface beneath her feet. The girl then rises before Lynleit. She remains silent and tilts her head because a person standing on water falls outside the rule by which she takes victims. Lynleit is equally bewildered. Only Kyrien witnesses Lynleit standing on the river and keeps the ability secret afterward. Lynleit later reaches him on the park side, where they recover among the trees before rejoining the others. Institutional readings Police and government Darkness, panic, current, exhaustion, and shared misperception can be used to separate the officers' accounts from the empty boats and missing smugglers. No ordinary report can explain why several trained swimmers independently describe hands pulling at their legs. Magi and special envoys An embodied Holumn has enslaved the river's drowned souls and uses them as both grasping limbs and a collective voice. Blue flame can injure the submerged hands, and the hands cannot cross the surface layer. Both limits permit escape without establishing a means of destroying the manifestation or releasing the dead. The River That Is Too Deep Record: HI-004 Known forms: Environmental and possibly embodied Primary medium: The city river The river produces waves its width and depth should not permit. Boats and kayaks suffer damage without a sufficient material cause. Bodies recovered from the water carry missing sections larger than the bite of any animal expected in the river. The available evidence does not yet establish whether a creature occupies the river, whether the river itself has become the manifestation, or whether both readings describe different layers of the same Holumn. Institutional readings Police and government Hidden debris, dangerous currents, criminal interference, and postmortem animal damage remain the available categories. Magi and special envoys The damage may come from a Holumn whose movement does not fit the river's measured depth. Whether this is a creature, a change in the river, or both remains disputed. The Nameless Street Record: HI-005 Known forms: Environmental, event-bound, and possibly curse-bound Primary medium: An untraceable street in the old town of central Vilen The Nameless Street is an urban myth among visitors to Vilen. Under unknown conditions, a person who becomes lost may enter a deserted network of steep lanes, stairs, courtyards, balconies, retaining walls, and sudden drops that cannot be reconciled with the surrounding city. The warning attached to the story is simple: do not follow anyone encountered there. Those who follow may never return to ordinary streets. Days before Fionn's death, Lynleit is walking with Felix after lunch when she finds herself alone. She is dizzy, unable to walk straight, and suffering a severe headache. A little girl carrying a red balloon appears. When the balloon escapes, the girl runs away crying. Lynleit catches its thread and follows the girl's cries through the labyrinth so she can return it. The girl eventually stands beside a broken fence above an abrupt fall. A dead boy lies below. Lynleit releases the balloon in shock. The girl smiles and pushes her from the ledge. Before Lynleit strikes the ground, she wakes on a bench in the ordinary city center. Felix is fanning her face with a piece of paper and describes only a fainting episode. He did not enter the street. Several days later, Lynleit sees Fionn's body below the hill at the family house. The memory of the dead boy returns before she can control her reaction. Helena uses that genuine shock to support the false accusation that Lynleit pushed her father. Institutional readings Police and government Felix's account supports a sudden loss of consciousness followed by a vivid dream, hallucination, or neurological episode. No second witness, traceable route, girl, balloon, or dead boy establishes a physical street. Magi and special envoys The street itself may be the Holumn. It isolates one visitor, replaces navigable urban space with a hostile sequence, and presents a lure whose pursuit ends at a fatal fall. It remains unknown whether Lynleit physically entered another place, experienced an event imposed on consciousness, or occupied both conditions at once. Doom Has an Address Read the Chapter Record: HI-006 Known forms: Event-bound and curse-bound Primary medium: The conscious identity of whoever destroys the Holumn Lynleit and Kyrien destroy the same Holumn together. Its death completes rather than ends its governing rule. The terminal condition transfers to the ego responsible for destroying it, and their joint action causes one curse to recognize both people as a single causal answer. The condition progresses over several weeks. Sleep ceases to restore either subject, minor injuries heal slowly, magical tolerance declines, and ordinary exertion becomes difficult. Suppression fails in both directions: removing the condition from Lynleit allows Kyrien's attachment to reconstruct it, while removing it from Kyrien allows Lynleit's attachment to do the same. The established answer requires one subject to die first. Permanent loss of either ego collapses the two-person relation and releases the survivor. Lynleit refuses that solution and pursues Magiarchal, theurgical, academic, and Church accounts of curses attached to identity. Natalia introduces the ego hypothesis and quotes Jung's definition of conscious identity to explain what she believes the curse recognizes. Father Mikhail finds related Church records in which conversion, marriage, war, parenthood, or confession changed a subject deeply enough to disrupt a psychic attachment. Both conclude that biological death is the most reliable identity discontinuity, but not the only one. Lynleit attempts intimacy with Kyrien without telling him about the proposed treatment. The encounter is not completed. The curse begins weakening the following morning and later disappears. The attempt and its aftermath change both identities enough to defeat its recognition; a completed sexual act is not required. Kyrien remains unaware of the proposed method. Institutional readings Police and government The visible case consists of two people developing the same rapid decline after an operation. Medicine can document the symptoms and treatment failures but cannot explain why intervention in one patient is reversed through the other. Magi and special envoys The Holumn stores its death in the identity of its killer. A joint killing gives the curse two coordinates. It can be broken by death or by a transformation severe enough that the original identities can no longer be recognized as the complete answer to the act. The destroyed Holumn's appearance, origin, prior incident history, and the operation that brings Lynleit and Kyrien into contact with it remain unidentified. Victims and Incident Witnesses,Archive

entries.title: Magecraft: Structure, Leverage, and Cost
entries.subtitle: Magecraft Doctrine
entries.text: Magecraft: Structure, Leverage, and Cost Magecraft Doctrine A practical guide to magecraft mechanics, internal and external practice, limitations, Holumn manifestations, and the need for control. Magecraft: Structure, Leverage, and Cost Magecraft and miracle-making Magecraft uses conditions already present in reality. A Magus perceives a point of strain or weakness and deliberately alters it. Fire can be encouraged to start, matter weakened, attention sharpened, or perception redirected. The effect requires something to act upon. Miracle-making is a separate, forbidden category. The Church condemns acts that imitate sacred deeds associated with Jesus, saints, saviours, and other religious figures, even when the immediate effect is harmless. Lynleit's water walking falls within this prohibition. Two directions of practice Thaumaturgy Thaumaturgy acts outward upon the surrounding world. Its effects can usually be observed or measured. Igniting or suppressing fire Reinforcing or weakening material Changing concentration or distribution Altering physical sensation Redirecting an environmental process Theurgy Theurgy acts upon the operator's perception, thought, identity, or relationship to the world. Expanding awareness Altering perception Recalibrating thought and emotion Integrating spiritual experience Changing the way identity is understood An inward change can carry risks as serious as a visible physical intervention. The continuum Thaumaturgy and theurgy are categories within one connected reality. An outward spell requires an adjustment in its operator. A change in perception or identity changes how that person acts upon the world. Matter, perception, emotion, probability, agency, and cognition belong to the same natural structure. The distinction between inward and outward practice describes the principal direction of an act, not a complete separation. Magi Magi are human. Their unusual perception lets them identify conditions that other people cannot detect, and their training lets them intervene deliberately. Talent is rare and unevenly distributed. Training alone does not guarantee it. Power depends on both perception and control. Fionn's precise blue flame and Lynleit's dangerous volume illustrate different uses of the same inherited ability. Holumn manifestations Fear, memory, fixation, and psychic strain can produce Holumns. The source may be an individual or a population, and its manifestation need not be a creature. Weather, events, disembodied wills, and curses also belong to the category. A visible body may be only one part of a manifestation. Containment therefore requires evidence about its circumstances, repeated conditions, people, and objects as well as its physical form. Incident records and known countermeasures are collected in Holumns. Limits and cost Magecraft cannot create something from nothing or erase the foundational conditions upon which it works. Every intervention changes an existing balance and can meet resistance. Overuse can destabilize the affected system. Poor judgment can direct force into the wrong place. Greater force increases exposure to backlash. A successful effect can cause harmful secondary consequences. Precision can achieve what a larger display cannot. Its value depends on the operator understanding the conditions well enough to avoid unwanted effects. Authority and secrecy The Magiarchy regulates sanctioned practice and cooperates with the Church in containment. The Church needs Magi to suppress threats ordinary institutions cannot handle, but watches for uncontrolled practice and forbidden miracles. Renegade Magi reject the arrangement. Both the Church and the Magiarchates pursue them. Most people do not know magic exists. Some clergy, officials, and advisers receive limited knowledge. The Church holds final sanction over suppression; Magiarchal resources may investigate, contain, coerce, recruit, or remove witnesses under that authority. Exposure can provoke Church retaliation, public panic, or conflict inside Magi institutions. Disagreement over what to conceal and how to conceal it persists within the sanctioned order. Magistry Archive

entries.title: MAGIARCHY Prose Style · v1
entries.subtitle: Writer's Style Reference
entries.text: MAGIARCHY Prose Style · v1 Writer's Style Reference The working house style: narrative voice, focalization, comic timing, dialogue, rhythm, imagery, and reader inference, developed through the Chapters. MAGIARCHY Prose Style This is the working house style for Chapters. Its starting point is the author's preference for concrete scenes, unruly conversation, unsettling supernatural rules, and intimacy that intrudes on a story concerned with other things. It develops through actual Chapters rather than through imitation of another writer. Use this document alongside Prose and Scene Guidance, which owns revision boundaries and development approaches. This document owns narrative voice and craft choices. Narrative voice and focalization Default: third-person past tense with a clearly established focal character. Let the narration borrow that person's vocabulary and immediate concerns through free indirect discourse, without turning every thought into an italicized monologue. Stay close during fear, embarrassment, discovery, and difficult decisions. A character can notice a wet cuff before understanding a curse. Widen the psychic distance for travel, repeated failed attempts, elapsed time, or a rule already established in the scene. Change focalization at a section or scene break. In Doom Has an Address, Lynleit's research and Kyrien's incomplete account require separate access to their thoughts. Neither should know what the other has concealed simply because the narrator does. The narrator may be dry, observant, and briefly amused. Comic commentary is welcome when it sharpens a particular absurdity. Avoid an omniscient verdict that explains what every gesture proves about the cast. Tonal register and counterpoint The principal register combines precise observation with conversational ease. Technical language belongs to a character solving a technical problem; it should not become everyone's inner voice. Let terror, ordinary inconvenience, and embarrassment occupy the same scene without cancelling one another. The fatal curse remains fatal while Lynleit objects to the proposed solution. A lost jacket can matter to her without being the emotional thesis of the river chapter. Humor often comes from unequal seriousness: the answer is technically useful, socially unbearable, and delivered by someone enjoying that discrepancy. Do not make every character equally witty. Reiner need not return Felix's joke; Kyrien's plain question can cause more trouble than a clever retort. The Nasu advisory framework may help test a rule, exception, or dramatic consequence. It does not supply a borrowed voice, stock catchphrase, or permission to imitate a particular author's prose. Scene, summary, and exposition Dramatize the point where someone must answer, act, refuse, or reconsider. Summarize the travel and repeated research that bring them there. A supernatural explanation earns space when it changes the available choices. Natalia's explanation of the ego is a discovery in this scene, not background terminology the narrator should give Lynleit beforehand. Mikhail contributes a different body of evidence before giving an embarrassingly practical answer. Preserve the discovery sequence : observation, interpretation, objection, revised possibility. Let an explanation meet resistance. The listener may interrupt for the wrong reason, misunderstand a word, or resent a perfectly accurate answer. “Show, don't tell” is a preference for dramatizing important experience, not a ban on exposition. State a mechanism plainly when withholding it would confuse the scene. Do not then explain its emotional meaning after the reader has already watched the reaction. Dialogue, idiolect, and subtext Speech should carry at least one immediate purpose: obtain an answer, evade it, test a premise, provoke, reassure, delay, or end the conversation. The purpose need not match what the speaker admits. Lynleit Idiolect: specific questions, impatient objections, attempts to return a discussion to its useful conclusion. She can handle professional disclosure yet become evasive when the subject is personally embarrassing. Repeated denials may expose what she intends to close. Natalia Idiolect: precise definitions, associative examples, a former teacher's questions, and dry corrections. She enjoys making Lynleit follow a sound argument to an unwelcome conclusion. Do not remove her playfulness in order to make her seem intelligent. Father Mikhail Idiolect: patient doctrinal explanation followed by unexpectedly blunt ordinary language. He continues giving useful advice while Lynleit is trying to escape the conversation. His irreverence does not erase his conviction or severity elsewhere. Kyrien Idiolect: short questions, literal observation, suspicion when someone's behavior changes. He can recognize that something happened without possessing the missing explanation. Frustration does not require a confession or an eloquent speech. These are observations from the current Chapters, not scripts for every future line. MBTI and function emphasis support a characterization check; they do not dictate syntax or replace personal history. Prefer unobtrusive dialogue tags. Use action beats when they locate a speaker, change the timing, or reveal divided attention. A page turned without being read does more here than several descriptions of hidden desire. Comic timing and repetition Distinguish redundant exposition from comic repetition . Repeated information can be cut; a repeated denial may be the action of the scene. Preserve the setup, escalation, pause, reversal, and closing beat when revising a comic exchange. Read it aloud before removing a line. In Doom Version 3: The examination routine restores the old teacher-student relationship before Natalia supplies the ego hypothesis. The academically respectable answer sets up the instruction to consult a priest. Mikhail's apparent consideration of centuries of theology delays an exceptionally blunt answer. His repeated use of Lynleit's name accompanies successive stages of her exit. “It worked” and “By failing” make the same recovery mean different things to the speakers. The later “I haven't asked anything” exchange recalls the earlier call. The repetition now exposes Lynleit's anticipation. Natalia's final question works because the preceding silence has made Lynleit keep talking. Do not compress this into a summary that says Natalia teased her. Do not explain the punchline afterward. A joke may need several apparently unnecessary lines to establish its timing. Syntax, rhythm, and paragraphing Use complete, varied sentences for the narrative baseline. Alternate longer sentences that follow observation or reasoning with shorter sentences at a decision or interruption. Short paragraphs and fragments are emphasis tools. A whole chapter of isolated declarations gives every detail the same weight. Dialogue can remain one utterance per paragraph because the white space controls turn-taking and pace. Use a deliberately repeated structure for a specific effect, then leave it. Avoid habitual three-part lists, mirrored reversals, and final sentences that restate the paragraph in grander language. Keep tense consistent unless a quoted document or deliberate temporal shift requires otherwise. No em dashes. Diction and imagery Prefer concrete verbs, recognizable materials, and specific physical relationships. Fishing line, a soaked sleeve, an unread page, and a notebook are useful because someone can touch or act on them. Choose imagery through focalization. Lynleit may notice dress and composure; Kyrien may notice a change in someone's movements. Neither should become an all-purpose sensor reporting every detail. Use an extended metaphor only while it helps the reader reason. Natalia's address metaphor makes the curse's recognition understandable; it should not spread into every description of affection, leadership, or domestic life. Do not justify an appearance or defend a character after every flawed response. Do not label an ordinary feeling as profound. Leave room for awkwardness that remains awkward. Subtext, ellipsis, and reader knowledge Subtext is what a reader can infer from speech, behavior, juxtaposition, or omission. It is not a fact the author has not decided yet. Ellipsis may omit an encounter while showing its consequences. Doom Version 3 does not narrate the incomplete attempt itself. The next call and Kyrien's account establish what they can establish; exact choreography remains unresolved. Mark Chapter preface and Moment conclusions as inferred only when the scene supplies evidence without stating the conclusion. If a revision makes the explanation explicit, change the label. Do not explain a purple inference in narration merely to make it easier to validate. Keep later consequences out of an earlier scene's closing summary unless a flash-forward is a deliberate narrative choice. Terminology and researched allusion Physicians are ordinary medical professionals without knowledge of magic unless the author explicitly establishes an exception. Do not invent a class of physicians treating thaumaturgy. A medical examination, if used, must preserve that ignorance and show or account for concealment. Doom Version 3 uses Magi's examination of the curse and does not add an off-page physician visit. Natalia introduces the ego hypothesis and attributes the psychological definition to Jung. Her application of it to the curse belongs to fictional magecraft, not to Jung's claim. Brief quotations must be verified; store their source here rather than interrupting dialogue with research apparatus. The short definition quoted in Version 3 is reproduced in the C. G. Jung Society of Sydney's account of ego, shame, and embodiment. Only that definition is quoted. The curse mechanism and Natalia's proposed use of reciprocal change are fictional. Revision protocol Before drafting or editing a Chapter or Moment, read this document, the chosen source version, and the relevant character records. Identify the focal character, discovery sequence, emotional pressure, and any dialogue whose timing must survive. During revision, keep two separate passes: 1. Dramatic pass: continuity, knowledge, choices, voice, discovery, and the function of each exchange. 2. Line-edit pass: cadence, diction, repetition, dialogue tags, paragraphing, and unnecessary explanation. Compare the result against the source. Restore any lost joke, disagreement, or character-specific awkwardness that was removed merely for concision. Recheck the preface, Moment, and F/M/S anchors against the actual revised paragraphs. Afterward, add a concise entry below only when the Chapter teaches us a reusable style choice. Give its source, craft term, example or location, and limit. Separate author decisions from editorial working choices. Do not accumulate a new absolute rule for every attractive sentence. Style decisions in use Author direction: 5 September 2026 Preserve original banter and comic repetition. Natalia originates the ego idea and quotes Jung. Do not introduce magic-aware physicians. Limit: a joke's timing does not excuse duplicate explanations elsewhere. Working implementation: Doom Has an Address, Version 3 Past-tense narration, sectioned focalization, exposition through adversarial dialogue, callbacks, exit beats, and an elliptical encounter. Limit: these devices do not require every Chapter to be comic or withhold its central action. Under review: later Chapters Refine the house style from what the author accepts in finished scenes. Limit: no new event or character trait becomes canon through this document. Version 3 is based on the earlier Version 2 text preserved in commit 868fc31 , before the prose rewrite in b06c821 . It restores that dialogue-led treatment, applies the author's corrections, and is now the canonical version. Versions 1 and 2 remain accessible alternates. Author's Desk

entries.subtitle: Editorial Reference
entries.text: Prose and Scene Guidance · v1 Editorial Reference Revision principles, content boundaries, and author-favored development approaches kept separate from established canon. Prose and Scene Guidance For narrative voice, dialogue, rhythm, comic timing, and a log of Chapter-specific style choices, use MAGIARCHY Prose Style alongside every draft. This document owns revision boundaries and development approaches. This is editorial guidance. It does not add events, motives, or supernatural rules to canon. Established facts belong in their archive records; a Chapter lets the reader experience them. Revision priorities Keep the particular image, gesture, joke, or inconvenience. Remove an explanation when the scene has already communicated it. Do not follow every strong line with a stronger-sounding conclusion. Ordinary sentences give an interruption or startling image room to register. Keep interpretation close to a character's knowledge. A frightened or mistaken conclusion is useful; an omniscient verdict about everyone involved often ends the uncertainty too early. Preserve different speech habits. Felix can keep a joke going; Reiner can decline to participate. Natalia may pursue a definition while Lynleit wants an answer. Kyrien may answer plainly and fail to reassure anyone. Do not defend a competent character after every bad reaction. Competence, affection, embarrassment, selfishness, and poor judgment can coexist. Give each consultation a new piece of evidence, a failed treatment, a limitation, or a disagreement. Do not have several experts repeat one explanation in different vocabularies. Use MBTI to check a portrayal, not as its vocabulary. People do not need to think about their relationships as systems, access, or control merely because those terms helped an audit. Where information belongs Chapters: action, perception, dialogue, and character interpretation. Keep later revelations out of an earlier scene's closing explanation unless a deliberate flash-forward is part of the intended structure. Wiki records: identity, properties, history, limits, and known uncertainty. Describe what a coat does, not what preserving the coat achieves for the writer. Moments: concise scene facts, continuity, and reader knowledge. A later consequence may remain in continuity even when it is removed from the Chapter itself. Editorial Docs: alternatives, missing facts, unresolved contradictions, and proposed effects on the reader. An attractive proposal is not evidence that an event happened. Character timelines use short summaries tied to named events. Biography carries the fuller history. Connections describe the relationship; conflicts state a specific unresolved pressure. No section needs generic filler to look complete. Preferred development approaches These preserve earlier author-favored directions without making every unanswered question demand the same kind of answer. Institutions and conspiracies Give factions defensible but incompatible aims. Several people can contribute to Fionn's death without sharing a complete plan. The frame against Lynleit can rely on true observations placed in a false causal order. Fionn's caution and Helena's exclusion should have concrete consequences rather than receive moral verdicts from the narrator. The author favors old rules meeting unforeseen cases, limited Church authority with severe consequences, and MSF's mutual dependence with the state. Use these where an actual decision needs them. A rank, contract, or procurement detail can remain brief when no choice depends on it. Investigations and supernatural evidence A small observation may distinguish Drake. Evidence that Heyk cannot make useful to an institution may explain his need for unconventional allies. Natalia and Lester can understand different parts of one case. Experts on the Spill may each possess only part of the explanation. Separate a disappearance's mechanism, destination, and possibility of return when that preserves a worthwhile mystery. Keep uncertainty honest: if the author has not decided the answer, do not label it a conclusion the reader should infer. Places and domestic life Earlier directions connect the park's vulnerability to its history, the house's old name to a personal memory, and the river's aftermath to a lasting change. A room may have a restriction learned through behavior rather than exposition. These are development directions, not permission to invent a history or supernatural effect. Keep room for tea, laundry, clothes, the cat, and ordinary irritation. Such details do not need to be turned into symbols each time they appear. The relative entrusted with the child can be reliable without being someone Lynleit finds easy company. Relationships Let repeated work, arguments, games, and ordinary contact establish the pair before a crisis intensifies it. Trust does not explain every attraction. Felix may come to understand Kyrien without liking him; Natalia's refusal of a case may say more than another successful examination. Use a private gesture in the hotel refuge only if it fits Lynleit's immediate exhaustion. Do not insert a prescribed tender beat merely because the scene is important to the couple. Her duty and the main story remain primary. Current version decision Doom Has an Address Version 3 is canon. It restores the pre-rewrite Version 2's banter while correcting the physician references and making Natalia the source of the ego hypothesis and Jung quotation. The attempt at intimacy is incomplete. Both survive after the attempt and its aftermath change the identities to which the curse is attached. Their first completed sexual encounter belongs later in Arc 1. Versions 1 and 2 remain alternates and must not supply shared character or Holumn facts where they differ. Author's Desk

entries.text: Questions to Be Answered Editorial Ledger Confidence-tracked current canon and chronology questions, separated to support both worldbuilding and timeline placement. Questions to Be Answered This is the author's living editorial ledger. It separates unresolved canon questions from questions that determine placement on the shared Story and character timelines. Each unresolved question carries a confidence score based only on confirmed material. Answers belong in the wider site architecture, not in these tables. Questions that have been answered or made redundant are removed. Preferred development approaches are preserved in Prose and Scene Guidance, separate from the missing facts listed here. entries.title: The Duchy of Narvea
entries.subtitle: Country Profile
entries.text: The Duchy of Narvea Country Profile A concise visual guide to the mapped Baltic country where the story takes place, including its cities, diplomatic legacy, divided authority, institutions, and multilingual culture. The Duchy of Narvea At a glance The Duchy of Narvea is the main country in which the story takes place. It is a large, sovereign Baltic state stretching along much of the eastern Baltic coast, from the approaches to St. Petersburg toward the frontier near Gdansk. Narvea is a constitutional duchy with two real centers of authority: the Ducal Crown and the parliamentary state . The Duke is an independent sovereign, not a subordinate noble. Parliament and the Prime Minister control ordinary government. Sovereignty resides jointly in the Crown and the Nation. Identity Narvean is a civic identity shared across a culturally varied population. Citizens may belong to different regional, linguistic, religious, urban, or rural communities while identifying fully and politically as Narvean. The country modernized without erasing its older institutions. Modern ministries, elections, police, and armed forces exist beside a ducal court, inherited ranks, ceremonial precedence, and a separate Ducal Guard. European diplomacy Narvea historically became a center of European diplomacy. Opposing powers gathered there to resolve disputes before they escalated into open conflict, giving the duchy influence far beyond its size or military strength. During the Napoleonic Wars of 1803 to 1815, Narvea played an important and constructive role in containing the continental crisis. The settlements of this period also began shaping the country's borders into their modern form. In 1917, negotiations held in Narvea contained an eastern political crisis before it could become a revolution. In 1939, another Narvean settlement stopped escalation between opposing powers and prevented a major continental war. These agreements allowed continental borders and political history to develop along a different course. That diplomatic legacy made multilingualism part of Narvean public culture. People in authority are expected to know several languages, but the custom is not limited to officials. Ordinary Narveans may switch languages during everyday conversation for precision, courtesy, emphasis, or habit, even when diplomacy is nowhere near the room. Bird's Nest, the city with many names Most negotiations between rival nations take place in Bird's Nest. Foreign countries use their own names for the city; Bird's Nest is its Narvean name. Territory Long Baltic coastline and several major ports Important agricultural regions and trade routes Multiple linguistic, religious, and cultural regions Strategic frontier with Russia Strong commercial and military importance in the Baltic The country's exact borders are not fully recorded. The two capitals Rennel Rennel, in the historic Narva region, is the seat of the Crown. It contains the Ducal Palace, court, Privy Council, Guard headquarters, dynastic archives, heraldic offices, and ceremonial institutions. Vilen Vilen is the parliamentary and administrative capital. It contains Parliament, the Prime Minister's office, ministries, major courts, central bureaucracy, and financial institutions. The Prime Minister travels to Rennel for formal audiences with the Duke. The Duke travels to Vilen for major constitutional ceremonies, including the opening of Parliament. Turon Turon is a significant city and the headquarters of MSF. MSF is a fully private intelligence business that sells its services to the government while retaining control of its own succession and internal affairs. A substantial part of its officer corps is concentrated in Turon, giving the company a degree of local power that quietly troubles the central government. If MSF ever chose open defiance, its presence in Turon could support a small rebellion or even an attempt at secession. Officer culture, divided logistics, constitutional loyalty, and the absence of any desire to rebel keep that capacity dormant. Politicians know that the final safeguard is officer decency, not an enforceable external restraint. Crown and State The Ducal Crown The Duke is head of state and constitutional guardian. He appoints the Prime Minister who holds parliamentary confidence, promulgates laws, receives ambassadors, grants honours, consults the Privy Council, commands the Ducal Guard, and may hold narrowly defined reserve powers. The parliamentary state The Prime Minister is head of government. Parliament, Cabinet, ministries, the civil service, courts, police, and national armed forces handle ordinary administration, taxation, defence policy, education, infrastructure, economic policy, and foreign policy. Security institutions Narvean Armed Forces The national military is funded by the state and controlled through the constitutional government. It may include the Army, Navy, Air Force, reserves, territorial forces, and military intelligence. Ducal Guard The Ducal Guard belongs to the Crown. It protects the ducal family and residences, guards Crown institutions, performs ceremonial duties, and may have limited constitutional-security responsibilities. Narvean Police Ordinary policing belongs to the parliamentary state, most likely under the Ministry of the Interior. Palace security remains separate from public law enforcement. Councils and service rank The Privy Council advises the Duke on constitutional questions, foreign affairs, national security, appointments, dynastic matters, and emergencies. It does not replace Cabinet or Parliament. The Council of State bridges Crown and government through constitutional review, administrative law, senior appointments, disputes, and emergency continuity. Its unresolved jurisdiction becomes most important when ordinary constitutional sovereignty collides with hidden supernatural authority that the public state cannot formally acknowledge. Narvea retains its own hierarchy of court and civil ranks. Rank determines precedence and status, but does not necessarily describe a person's actual job. A State Councillor might serve as an ambassador, judge, governor, rector, or senior ministry official. Drake holds the rank of State Councillor and the office of Official for Special Assignments. He is an elite executive troubleshooter attached to a high-ranking personal office and is free from routine administration. He can carry delegated authority into confidential criminal investigations, political counter-espionage, emergency corruption audits, and diplomatic errands. His friendship with the Duke begins when Drake is the only official willing to tell him that he is wrong. That refusal to flatter earns exceptional access and occasional forgiveness, but later makes Drake deeply unpopular at Court, where courtiers deride him as the Duke's pampered favorite. Cultural character Narvea carries layered coastal, inland, courtly, mercantile, urban, rural, and frontier traditions. Catholic and Orthodox communities coexist across regions with distinct architecture, memory, dialect, and politics. The central tension Narvea lives through a permanent partnership, and occasional rivalry, between inherited continuity and popular government. A modern minister can hold an old civil rank. A national officer can attend a ceremony governed by ducal precedence. An elected Prime Minister controls policy but still travels to the palace for a formal audience. Narvean State Archive

entries.title: What Can You Tell Me About Magi?
entries.subtitle: Magistry
entries.text: What Can You Tell Me About Magi? Magistry A dialogue on the nature, secrecy, religion, and politics of Magi. What Can You Tell Me About Magi? Journalist: "What can you tell me about Magi?" Fionn: "What do you already know?" Journalist: "That you can do things other people cannot. Nobody will tell me how." Fionn: "We perceive conditions most people miss. With training, we can alter them. Encourage a fire, weaken material, redirect attention. The result may look impossible to someone who cannot see how it was done." Journalist: "So it is natural." Fionn: "It occurs within nature. That doesn't make it safe." Journalist: "And miracles?" Fionn: "A separate question. The Church considers certain acts an imitation of sacred miracles. A harmless result can still be forbidden." Journalist: "Who decides what counts?" Fionn: "The Church has a considerable interest in that decision." Journalist: "You sound less certain than before." Fionn: "I'm describing an agreement, not a law of physics." Journalist: "Why keep all this secret?" Fionn: "Because the institutions containing it depend on secrecy. A witness can expose people, methods, and threats we have not learned to control." Journalist: "Does that mean the witness has to die?" Fionn: "It means the authorities will consider how to prevent the exposure." Journalist: "Including killing them." Fionn: "Yes." Journalist: "Would you?" Fionn: "You have not given me a case." Journalist: "I have given you a person." Fionn: "And I have not given you permission to assume the decision is simple." Journalist: "The Church approves these decisions?" Fionn: "It holds final sanction over suppression. Magi have resources the Church needs, and powers it has reason to fear. Cooperation has not removed either fact." Journalist: "Then the Church rules you." Fionn: "A Magiarch governs a territory. There is no lawful universal ruler of Magi." Journalist: "Could the Magiarchs organize one?" Fionn: "Not without breaking the arrangement with the churches." Journalist: "That sounds political." Fionn: "It is." Journalist,Fionn

entries.title: Doom Has an Address
entries.subtitle: HI-006 · Operational encounter and curse
entries.text: Doom Has an Address HI-006 · Operational encounter and curse HI-006 doom-has-an-address Doom Has an Address Operational encounter and curse event curse A Holumn transfers its own terminal condition to whoever consciously destroys it. When Lynleit and Kyrien kill it together, one fatal curse identifies both egos as a single causal answer and remains distributed across them. Fatigue, slow healing, and persistent exhaustion appear as a physical illness to anyone unaware of the curse. The linked decline has no explanation within that account. Natalia identifies the attachment as recognition of the ego, using Jung's definition of conscious identity. A joint killing gives the curse two subjects, each capable of restoring the condition in the other while both remain recognizably the same people. The subjects weaken over several weeks. Sleep ceases to restore them, injuries heal too slowly, Lynleit's magecraft becomes exhausting, and ordinary exertion eventually becomes difficult. Suppressing either attachment causes the other to restore it. The curse begins weakening the morning after Lynleit and Kyrien's incomplete attempt at intimacy and later disappears. The curse requires exact sympathetic recognition of the ego or egos responsible for the Holumn's destruction. Biological death breaks that identity absolutely, but profound reciprocal transformation can introduce enough uncertainty to fracture the attachment without killing either subject. Destroying this Holumn transfers its fatal condition to its killers. Lynleit and Kyrien survive after an incomplete attempt at intimacy changes both identities enough to break its recognition. story.html?chapter=doom-has-an-address event,curse

entries.title: The Drowned Choir
entries.subtitle: HI-003 · Operational encounter
entries.text: The Drowned Choir HI-003 · Operational encounter HI-003 the-drowned-choir The Drowned Choir Operational encounter embodied environmental A pale girl rises from the river with her eyes sewn shut by fishing line and a dress made from dead fish. She enslaves the souls of people drowned in the river and uses their hands to pull new victims beneath the surface. Maren and the surviving officers report trained swimmers being pulled down by an unexpected force. Darkness, panic, dangerous current, exhaustion, and mutually reinforced testimony remain the available material explanations, while the empty contraband boats provide no visible attacker. The girl is an embodied Holumn controlling the river's accumulated drowned souls. The dead reach through the water as her hands and speak through her as the Drowned Choir. Submerged hands seize swimmers by the legs and pull downward. Lynleit's blue flame burns them even beneath the water and forces their grip open. They cannot pass through the surface layer beneath her feet once her water walking manifests. The girl's tilted head reads as confusion when Lynleit remains above the river. The drowned hands can be injured by blue flame beneath the water and cannot reach through the river's surface. These limits let Lynleit escape their grasp, but no method of freeing the enslaved dead or defeating the girl is confirmed. The Drowned Choir takes the contraband crews before the boats reach the bridge. The current carries the empty vessels onward. embodied,environmental

entries.title: The Last Piece
entries.subtitle: HI-002 · Missing-person incident
entries.text: The Last Piece HI-002 · Missing-person incident HI-002 the-last-piece The Last Piece Missing-person incident event curse A puzzle purchased at a market compels its owner to finish it. When the final piece is placed, the owner disappears and enters the missing-persons archive. Investigators see a purchased object, a developed obsession, and a disappearance. The puzzle may be treated as an unrelated possession, a clue to voluntary flight, or an instrument used by another person. The compulsion and completion belong to the same rule. Placing the final piece completes the condition that permits the disappearance. Attention narrows into addiction. Completion is followed by permanent disappearance, while the object remains available to be found again. No countermeasure is confirmed. Refusing completion appears safer than solving the object, but the strength and transfer of the compulsion remain unknown. The puzzle ties a disappearance to an ordinary act: placing the final piece. event,curse

entries.title: The Nameless Street
entries.subtitle: HI-005 · Urban legend and direct encounter
entries.text: The Nameless Street HI-005 · Urban legend and direct encounter HI-005 the-nameless-street The Nameless Street Urban legend and direct encounter environmental event curse A lost visitor may enter a deserted old street whose lanes, stairs, courtyards, and hills cannot be reconciled with the surrounding city. Following anyone encountered there may prevent the visitor from returning to ordinary streets. Felix sees Lynleit stop responding, move toward a city bench, and faint after lunch. Dizziness, a severe headache, a dream, or a neurological episode can explain the only part of the incident another person directly observes. The street behaves as a place-bound Holumn whose body is an impossible route and whose rule uses isolation, pursuit, and a fatal fall. Whether the girl, the boy, and the red balloon belong permanently to that rule remains unknown. The visitor is separated without perceiving a threshold, becomes dizzy and disoriented, and cannot navigate the district by ordinary geometry. Lynleit follows a crying girl to a broken fence, is pushed toward a dead boy below, and returns to a city bench before impact. The urban warning instructs visitors not to follow anyone encountered on the street. It is not known whether refusing the lure guarantees escape or why Lynleit returns after following it. Lynleit cannot reconcile the street with Vilen's geography. The fall later recalls Fionn's death, but no causal connection between the two is established. environmental,event,curse

entries.title: The River That Is Too Deep
entries.subtitle: HI-004 · Accumulated incident pattern
entries.text: The River That Is Too Deep HI-004 · Accumulated incident pattern HI-004 the-river-that-is-too-deep The River That Is Too Deep Accumulated incident pattern embodied environmental Something immense moves beneath the city river despite stretches too shallow to contain it. Impossible waves damage boats and kayaks, while drowned bodies lose pieces to bites larger than any expected river predator could make. Each report can be separated into wake damage, submerged debris, boating accidents, postmortem animal activity, or exaggerated witness comparison. Together they remain difficult to explain without inventing a cause the river should not contain. The leviathan may be an animal-like Holumn, the river giving itself predatory mass, or a depth that exists only when the manifestation passes through it. The river behaves as though it can briefly contain a body larger than its physical depth. Water displacement, impact damage, and feeding traces persist after the shape itself is gone. No countermeasure is confirmed. Its dependence on the river may be a boundary, but it is not yet known whether the water contains the Holumn or belongs to it. The damage suggests a moving mass larger than the river's measured depth could contain. embodied,environmental

entries.title: The Voice on the Line
entries.subtitle: HI-001 · Victim testimony
entries.text: The Voice on the Line HI-001 · Victim testimony HI-001 the-voice-on-the-line The Voice on the Line Victim testimony disembodied curse Have you heard of a telephone call that answers to you in your own voice? At first I thought whoever was on the phone was repeating me. But it was my own voice. At first it felt like an echo, as all it did was repeat my words. But then it started calling me incessantly, and it was talking to me, in bizarre ways. In my own voice. Police and communications specialists would first investigate harassment, recording fraud, a compromised exchange, equipment failure, or a witness in psychological distress. Magi and special envoys treat the change from repetition to unsolicited speech as the decisive detail. Something learned the witness's voice, then began using it without the witness. The calls become incessant. The voice stops merely repeating the witness and begins speaking independently. No countermeasure is confirmed. The calls use an ordinary telephone line. No visible body accompanies the borrowed voice. disembodied,curse

entries.title: Leviathan-hide coat
entries.subtitle: IA-001 · Anomalous garment
entries.text: Leviathan-hide coat IA-001 · Anomalous garment A blue garment left to Lynleit through Fionn's concealed intervention. It changes form without accepting commands and shields only what Lynleit deliberately covers with it. Held by Lynleit Lynleit lynleit Fionn fionn Arranged the substitution before his death A material called the hide of leviathan The nature and source of the material are not identified. Blue coat Its familiar full-length form and the appearance in which Lynleit first understands what Fionn left her. Scarf A smaller form chosen by the garment without instruction from Lynleit. Blue suede jacket The garment can imitate the fitted jacket Lynleit lost during the Drowned Choir attack. Other clothing The coat can assume other wearable forms. Lynleit cannot choose which form appears on a given day. Minor magical protection The material can shield a covered body from minor magically induced damage and phenomena. Protection by coverage Wearing the garment is not sufficient. Lynleit must use it to cover the threatened part of her body. Protection of another person Lynleit can remove the garment and place or throw it over someone who needs immediate protection. Autonomous form The garment decides its own appearance. It does not respond to Lynleit's preference or tactical need. Protection is local to the area physically covered by the garment. The garment does not provide passive protection merely because Lynleit is wearing it. Lynleit cannot command its form or rely on it to assume the form most useful to the situation. The exact boundary of minor magically induced damage remains unknown. Arc 1 The river operation The lost jacket The Drowned Choir tears away Lynleit's fitted blue suede jacket while dragging her underwater. She later complains about losing it because she liked it. Arc 1 Middle of the main story Fionn's concealed substitution After Fionn's death, Lynleit discovers that he had discreetly replaced the blue coat she wore with the leviathan-hide garment. Arc 1 After the discovery An inherited protection Lynleit carries the garment after discovering its properties. It sometimes takes the form of the suede jacket she lost. Moment The Coat Fionn Left Behind moments.html?moment=the-coat-fionn-left-behind Lynleit discovers the substitution and the garment's properties. Chapter The Empty Boats Beneath the Bridge story.html?chapter=the-empty-boats-beneath-the-bridge The river operation in which Lynleit loses the jacket later imitated by the coat. entries.title: A Meeting Beyond Authority
entries.subtitle: MOM-005 · Unknowing Convergence
entries.text: A Meeting Beyond Authority MOM-005 · Unknowing Convergence At night on a hill overlooking Vilen, Sherie leads an illegal negotiation in which Drake seeks limited access to MSF resources without surrendering sensitive evidence. Sherie secures MSF assistance through negotiations neither the government nor Court has authorized. A hill overlooking Vilen Sherie believes her uncle when the Court does not. Sherie is Drake's niece and is training under him to become a diplomat. The approach to Lynleit is entirely Sherie's idea and strategy. Sherie develops the plan against Drake's wishes, persuades him to participate, and takes charge of the meeting and negotiations. Drake remains opposed to the illegal approach but attends after Sherie overcomes his resistance. After the negotiation succeeds, Sherie asks Drake to praise and pamper her for her first achievement. Drake still cannot decide whether an alliance with Lynleit is a strategic advantage or a dangerous mistake. Drake remains the story's main strategic mind before and after this event. The meeting takes place at night on a hill overlooking Vilen. Drake does not hand sensitive evidence to people outside the aristocratic circle. He and Sherie request access to selected MSF resources and capabilities in exchange for concessions or favors. Sherie and Drake bring Heyk as their bodyguard and confidant. Lynleit brings Felix, Reiner, and Kyrien as her bodyguards and confidants. The main negotiation belongs to Lynleit, Sherie, and a reluctant Drake, while the others contribute opinions and warnings. Lynleit regards the request as dangerous. Felix openly protests, while Kyrien stays silent and tests the suspected conspiracy against his own past grievances. What concessions or favors do Drake and Sherie offer for the confirmed river-surveillance operation? What access or resources does Lynleit refuse beyond the limited operation? What would finally convince Drake that the alliance should be preserved or abandoned? Sherie must persuade Drake that Lynleit is worth the legal and political danger of contact. Sherie claims praise and pampering for her success while Drake remains uncertain about what she has created. The private agreement then produces a narrow intelligence operation. The team may inspect the suspected shipment but cannot arrest anyone or seize material. Drake drake Sherie sherie Lynleit lynleit Felix felix Reiner reiner Kyrien kyrien Heyk heyk

entries.title: After the Failed Attempt
entries.subtitle: MOM-001 · The Hidden Wager
entries.text: After the Failed Attempt MOM-001 · The Hidden Wager Lynleit interrogates Kyrien after his failed attempt against an MSF-protected Magus politician nearly harms her, then converts his prison risk into a secret recruitment without telling him she was present. Lynleit recruits Kyrien under threat of imprisonment without revealing that his attack nearly harmed her. Police office Kyrien has made a failed attempt to assassinate a politician who belongs to the Magi world. The politician is under MSF protection when Kyrien makes the attempt. Lynleit is present and is almost harmed unintentionally during the failed attack. Lynleit knows Kyrien nearly harmed her, but Kyrien does not know she was present. Lynleit never tells Kyrien that his attempt placed her in danger. The immediate aftermath brings him into a police office. Lynleit conducts the interrogation. Lynleit invokes an extraordinary transfer clause in MSF's government service contract, drafted under Fionn for extraordinary threats. The transfer gives her control of Kyrien's case, and she does not disclose the secret recruitment to Fionn. Kyrien faces prison unless he agrees to become Lynleit's secret helper. His freedom remains conditional on accepting Lynleit's demands, leaving him confined to her whims. Lynleit's private strategy is to keep Kyrien as a secret trump card against Helena. The recruitment occurs within the first few chapters, well before Fionn's assassination. Lynleit acts because her intuition warns her of near-future danger before she has enough evidence to define it. Lynleit is Fionn's biological daughter. Helena is Lynleit's stepmother and Fionn's wife. Lynleit already suspects Helena of being an enemy despite that family relationship. Kyrien's father held an important position in Narvea's military. The targeted politician was involved in causing his father's death. Kyrien obtained the knowledge and tools for the attempt through his father's military background. The attempt fails solely because the politician belongs to the Magi world. The politician's survival later creates consequences for Lynleit. Lynleit notices Helena probing Fionn's schedules, visitors to the family house, trusted officers, and Lynleit's own travel. Lynleit suspects murder because Helena appears to be studying the family too carefully. What is the politician's name, office, and exact role in Kyrien's father's death? How does the surviving politician later retaliate against Lynleit? What initial cover story conceals Kyrien's release and unofficial MSF association? Kyrien's father's death, the politician's involvement, the MSF protection assignment, and the military knowledge behind the attempt still need connective scenes. Kyrien enters Lynleit's service unwillingly without knowing that the handler controlling his case was nearly harmed by his attack. Lynleit must later decide who, if anyone, can be trusted with the recruitment. The arrangement preserves him as hidden leverage against Helena through the early investigation. Fionn's much later assassination vindicates Lynleit's warning without proving that she understood its source. Lynleit lynleit Kyrien kyrien

entries.title: Ash in the Family House
entries.subtitle: MOM-002 · Vanishing Point
entries.text: Ash in the Family House MOM-002 · Vanishing Point Before the crisis reaches her home directly, Lynleit clumsily chases a grey male cat named Ash, catches him, then cannot bring herself to expel him into the rain. Lynleit catches Ash but lets him stay because it is raining. The Director's House The scene occurs in the early chapters, after danger has begun outside but before Lynleit's life starts to collapse. The grey cat is male and is named Ash. The family maintained an original house in Turon while Lynleit's mother was alive and Lynleit was in junior school. After her mother's death, the family moved to a Vilen residence for Fionn's access to the capital. Lynleit accepted the move only after securing the third-floor study-bedroom. The Vilen house is a three-floor family residence on a wooded hill above the river that flows toward the city center, with a small rear park and garden. Lynleit values the thick vegetation and the sound of leaves and branches in the wind. She regards nearby flowing water as life energy and seeks its emotional grounding despite her childhood fear of drowning. The garden-facing first floor contains glass-enclosed relaxation areas that preserve contact with nature through every season. Lynleit personally chases Ash through the house, revealing a clumsier and more childish side of her than her public role usually permits. Lynleit eventually catches Ash. She cannot bring herself to expel him because rain is falling outside. Ash decides to remain and becomes a permanent loiterer in the family home. Who else in the household accepts or resists Ash's permanent presence? The first disappearances have begun outside Lynleit's private life, but the full crisis, Fionn's death, and the destruction of her family security remain ahead. Ash remains inside the house as a quiet domestic echo of the danger Lynleit cannot keep outside. Later losses can turn the once-comic chase into an omen whose meaning becomes clear only in retrospect. Lynleit lynleit Ash ash

entries.title: Because There's a Battle to Be Fought
entries.subtitle: MOM-017 · Clear Her Name
entries.text: Because There's a Battle to Be Fought MOM-017 · Clear Her Name Lynleit asks Kyrien why he continues to help her and risk his life when no reward awaits him. He answers immediately: "Because there's a battle to be fought." Lynleit wants to spare Kyrien needless danger. He considers the fight sufficient reason to go. Unspecified Lynleit is bewildered by Kyrien's willingness to keep helping her and entering danger when no reward has been promised. She does not want to place him in danger without necessity. Kyrien answers bluntly and without hesitation: "Because there's a battle to be fought." For Kyrien, the existence of a battle is itself a reason to enter it. The impulse belongs to the same childish competitive streak that makes him want to win every game. Kyrien does not say that he is fighting for Lynleit, leaving the reader to judge how much of his persistence is self-directed and how much attachment has entered a motive he still describes as combat. inferred His need to prove his worth may be directed toward his own standards, the memory of his father, or both. inferred Which operation or immediate danger prompts Lynleit to ask the question? How does Lynleit respond to an answer that removes her from Kyrien's stated reason for staying? Does Kyrien understand at this point that attachment has become part of the battle he keeps choosing? Kyrien has repeatedly accepted danger beside Lynleit, but rescue, coercion, and operational necessity do not fully explain why he keeps returning. Lynleit can rely on Kyrien without mistaking his involvement for obedience or romance. His later free choice to remain after her authority fails confirms that the answer was not an excuse. Their second encounter is lighter and more playful because neither needs to deny that the first threshold occurred. What details at the opening of Arc 2 make the pregnancy inference clear without explaining or showing it directly? How much time passes between Doom Has an Address, their later encounters, the beginning of the pregnancy, and Lynleit's disappearance? In Doom Has an Address, an incomplete attempt at intimacy changes both of them enough to break the shared curse. Their sexual relationship begins later. entries.subtitle: MOM-010 · The Quarantine
entries.text: Beyond the Cordon MOM-010 · The Quarantine Hiyu enters the quarantined park to test his impossible suspicion that magic is involved in the disappearances. Yulia goes with him to prove the theory wrong and keep him alive. Hiyu's theory takes him and Yulia into a danger neither understands. The quarantined park in Vilen Hiyu and Yulia are university students in their mid-twenties who study criminology. Yulia is a classical ISTJ and the top student in their class, with meticulous command of detail and criminological protocol. Hiyu is an ENTP whose personal investigations rely on intuitive threads, improvised methods, and rapid hypothesis generation. Without knowing that magic exists, Hiyu suspects it is involved in the disappearances. Yulia enters partly to prove him wrong and partly to prevent him from facing the danger alone. How do they bypass the cordon? What do they find, and how do they survive or escape? What lasting evidence, injury, or change in their relationship follows the trespass? The widening disappearance case gives Hiyu enough fragments to form an impossible but directionally correct theory. Yulia rejects the conclusion but refuses to let him test it alone. Their evidence connects two civilian students to the larger institutional response. Hiyu correctly suspects magic but still lacks any complete knowledge of it. Hiyu hiyu Yulia yulia

entries.title: Doom Has an Address · Version 1 · Alternate
entries.subtitle: MOM-021 · Lynleit Disappears
entries.text: Doom Has an Address · Version 1 · Alternate MOM-021 · Lynleit Disappears After Lynleit and Kyrien destroy a Holumn together, its death becomes one terminal curse written across both identities. Research leads Lynleit to a form of survival that requires reciprocal change rather than either person's death. Turns the pair's accumulated trust and involuntary attraction into the mechanism of a Holumn conflict without making romance the story's primary objective. Natalia's scholarship and Father Mikhail's Church records independently identify transformation as the only survivable answer. Several locations, ending in a private room Lynleit and Kyrien consciously destroy the same Holumn together. Destroying the Holumn completes its mechanism and transfers its terminal condition to the ego responsible for its death. Their joint action leaves one curse distributed across two identities rather than creating two separate curses. Their bodies weaken, sleep stops restoring them, minor injuries heal slowly, magical tolerance declines, and ordinary exertion becomes increasingly difficult. Suppressing the condition in either person fails because the remaining attachment reconstructs it in the other. The traditional solution requires one of them to die first, collapsing the relation and releasing the survivor. Lynleit refuses to choose which of them should live and searches Magiarchal records, medicine, prohibited theurgy, Natalia's research, and Church records for another answer. Natalia identifies the curse as an attachment to conscious identity and explains that profound transformation may make the original ego unrecognizable to it. Father Mikhail independently confirms that conversion, marriage, war, parenthood, confession, and other identity-changing experiences have disrupted related curses. Mikhail tells Lynleit that sex could produce the necessary discontinuity only if a sufficient reciprocal attachment already exists. Although Lynleit normally treats openness as a leadership skill, she keeps this proposed solution from Kyrien because its sexual and personal implications embarrass her, and initially evaluates their relationship as a possible procedure. When their prognosis contracts from weeks to days, Lynleit initiates a sudden, clumsy, and almost argumentative encounter. Kyrien has enough time to understand what she is asking and responds deliberately. Their simultaneous and reciprocal crossing changes the identities recognized by the curse and makes its sympathetic attachment unstable. Sex is not itself the cure. The curse fractures because the encounter embodies a relationship change neither identity can dismiss as hypothetical. Both survive, but neither remains psychologically identical to the person who entered the battle. The final change leaves the reader to infer which former boundaries have ended and what ordinary shared life might become possible before Lynleit's disappearance. inferred What identity, appearance, and prior incident history belong to the Holumn before Lynleit and Kyrien destroy it? What operation places them in position to destroy it together? Which Magi first identify the traditional one-death solution, and how much of the prognosis becomes known outside the four people in this scene? Where does the final private encounter occur within late Arc 1? Lynleit and Kyrien have accumulated a private rhythm through work, cards, protected secrets, voluntary loyalty, and repeated physical awareness. Her original authority over him has already lost practical force, and he has chosen to remain. The curse fractures and both survive. Their short sexual relationship becomes part of an emerging shared life before Lynleit disappears near the Arc 2 threshold and her pregnancy becomes legible only at the opening of the next arc. entries.title: Father Mikhail Discovers the Breach
entries.subtitle: MOM-015 · Divided Attention
entries.text: Father Mikhail Discovers the Breach MOM-015 · Divided Attention Father Mikhail becomes the first authority to discover that Lynleit has shared forbidden knowledge of magic with outsiders. Kyrien corrects her attempt to limit the breach to himself by revealing that Felix and Reiner also know. Mikhail's discovery forces Lynleit to answer for the witnesses and contributes to MSF's later Magi role. Unspecified private location Father Mikhail is the first authority to learn that Lynleit has disclosed forbidden knowledge of magic to outsiders. Lynleit is unprepared for the discovery and promises to resolve the exposure on her own terms. Mikhail asks whether Kyrien is the only witness, and Lynleit reassures him. Kyrien immediately states that Felix and Reiner also know. Mikhail responds by looking at Lynleit in judgment rather than escalating the confrontation openly. Lynleit again promises to handle the problem in her own way. Mikhail leaves her with the warning: 'What you do is none of my business, but don't be surprised if I'll be sent to clean up your mess.' The encounter becomes an early cause of MSF's later transformation into a partly Magi private enterprise reporting to the Magiarchy and the Church. After Mikhail leaves, Lynleit confronts Kyrien privately for exposing Felix and Reiner. Kyrien does not apologize or retreat. Lynleit does not use her authority to punish him. Their delay in stepping apart lets the reader register unwanted physical awareness inside the argument without turning the institutional conflict into a romantic scene. inferred Kyrien remains to help Lynleit address the breach after the argument. Kyrien gives no reason for correcting Lynleit, leaving the reader to infer whether literal honesty, distrust of institutional half-truths, or another motive drives him. inferred Mikhail does not define his authority. His restraint and final warning imply that the Church may later send him back with powers he is not claiming in this conversation. inferred Where does the confrontation occur, and what evidence prevents Lynleit from denying the original disclosure? What action does Lynleit mean by handling the problem in her own way? What narrow authority would allow Mikhail to be sent back to clean up the breach? What formal agreement later makes MSF accountable to both the Magiarchy and the Church while preserving its private ownership? Lynleit has already allowed Kyrien, Felix, and Reiner to operate with knowledge that ordinary MSF officers and outsiders are forbidden to possess. Lynleit must create an institutional place for people she refuses to suppress or surrender. Kyrien's refusal to preserve her convenient half-truth creates personal friction, but he remains involved in solving the exposure. The eventual answer changes MSF's mandate and places part of the private company inside the Magiarchal and Church order.
